subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 4, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-143, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and the amendment of Mr. Skelly (p. 22957).

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I rise in what seems to be the usual Monday morning situation for this chamber, that of having closure imposed later on today. In this instance, closure is on a measure authorizing the Government to borrow some additional $19 billion. Our concern throughout the debate up to this point has been, in essence, the question of what the Government will do with the funds, specifically how and where they will employ them. From our point of view, where will the Government employ these funds to create jobs? Jobs are the single most important item facing the economy and our nation.
What will the Government do with this borrowing authority it is seeking? We know with some degree of certainty that with closure being imposed later on today we will probably never know where these funds will be used until we see the programs later on this year or next year. It is clear to many of us, not only on this side of the chamber but throughout this country, that whatever the Government does with this money, if in fact it does intend to use substantial portions to provide or to stimulate employment, it had better be used at least for midterm employment, if not, for long-term employment.
Many people in Canada are very concerned with the amount of money this Government has poured into winter make-work projects. These projects are of short-term duration and do little, if anything, to enhance permanent jobs for Canadians. That is our basic concern.
For Members such as myself I might be a little more willing to grant with an open mind the funds being sought by this Government if the funds were to be used in a way that left a legacy, be that legacy permanent job creation or the protection of our shipyards. Thousands are laid off in that industry. Many thousands are still working in our shipyards but their
future is bleak. If the Government were to direct some of that funding into that hard pressed industry, not only would it save the remaining jobs, but it would put many thousands now unemployed back to work.
The Government can restore these jobs by accelerating the Department of National Defence naval fleet replacement program, providing funds for the Canadian Coast Guard which requires fleet replacement as well as for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which also requires fleet replacement. Government accounts alone could restore 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the jobs that have been lost in the last two to three years in our Canadian shipyards. If the Government were to opt for that course, many of us on this side would perhaps be more willing to listen.
If it would use some of the funds to rid the transportation industry of the iniquitous fuel compensation charge, such as now applied to the marine and air industry, we might look upon this Bill more favourably. We read again in the press over the weekend about the dissatisfaction of the national air carriers with the Government's intention in the income tax Bill to press on through the back door with the collection of that tax. Hon. Members are aware of the marine industry's opinion of that tax. While this tax does not apply to road transportation, it is applied to shipping.
The Hon. C. D. Howe said in this Chamber: "What's a million?". We are talking about $1.5 million, but it may be just enough money to keep 2,000 to 3,000 Canadian seamen, marine engineers, mates and captains on the shore this shipping season. If some of the funds were directed toward the elimination of those two fuel taxes, then we might be more willing to grant the borrowing authority that the Government is seeking.
Another worth-while project for which these funds could be used is to provide the much-needed bridge pier fendering protection system for the seven bridges in this country that span navigable waters and are listed by the Government itself as posing a hazard to shipping and to the lives of those who use those bridges. I wonder if any of the funds will go into that project.
I doubt that anything will go into the expansion of the Canadian Armed Forces. We have heard much about bringing some of our young people into the Canadian Armed Forces for basic trade training purposes. That may go a long way, on a voluntary basis, and be very useful, but I doubt we will hear

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
anything about that here today. It is, however, another project of which we might approve.
What about search and rescue in Canada? Over the last ten years, very few topics have been as consistently brought before the House as that of search and rescue capacity and capability in Canada. The provision of some funds for the upgrading of this area would provide extra permanent jobs and expenditure in that area might encourage us to look somewhat more favourably on the Government's request for this money.
There are many other areas to be dealt with. We have only to cast our minds back to the disparaging and somewhat infuriating debate that has been perpetrated by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) with respect to offshore oil drilling rigs. For those men to be left out there for three weeks when there was, in fact, a danger to them is unacceptable to Canadians. There is no search and rescue capability present to take those men off those rigs in the event of danger. It is only in the last two or three days that we have seen the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, reluctantly or otherwise, order Mobil and others to bring their rigs ashore. That was an unacceptable situation. Indeed, it is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to make that type of decision, not the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, theoretically, knows absolutely nothing about wheather conditions, ship safety or ice movement. Where does he obtain his information? If we had better search and rescue facilities and better reporting capability, and if some of the $19 billion was to be used to provide that, thousands of Canadians would feel much better. However, we do not have that indication.
In looking to the future, unemployed Canadians do not yet have a hope of returning to permanment jobs in their trades. All they can look forward to is make-work programs, such as cutting out a hiking trail or painting the wicket fence around the ballpark or building another softball diamond. There is no money in the community, mind you, to sustain those facilities once they are built. If that is all they have to look forward to, and I am certain that to a large measure that is all they have to look forward to, then where can their hope be? Where is the hope for them? We hear grand talk about these people coming back into the labour force. They will come back into the labour force when the Government starts to spend the money available to it in the sustainment of the very few jobs which continue to exist in the traditional areas of commerce, industry and natural resources. They will not come back into industry for minimum wage, part-time work.
These are our concerns. Will some of the money go into industrial Cape Breton, where perhaps $1 billion is needed, or will there be just little piddling amounts for Mr. Gillespie and others of his ilk? We in Atlantic Canada need an ice-breaking capability for shallow draught harbours. We need it for safety and for the convenience of our fishermen. Is there any indication that it will be provided? Not a bit.
We regret that the Government has not taken the time to tell us, with some specific idea in mind, just how it will spend the money. As a result, it is our intention to vote against this measure later on this afternoon.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that at this stage we have only ten minutes in which to speak on the amendment to Bill C-143. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) should be congratulated. He has established a new record. Never before in the history of this country has anyone ever requested interim borrowing authority of $14 billion. It takes a lot of cheek to do that, especially when we do not even know what the money is for. That is what everyone on this side has been complaining about. We know we are in trouble, we know that revenues are down, and we know that the big tax grab on the petroleum industry has not paid off because people cannot afford gasoline to run their cars since they are not working. Due to the combination of the oil glut and the price drop, the Government is not deriving the revenue which it needs, and no one will deny that.
The point is that the Government is asking Parliament to agree to signing some kind of a blank cheque, and we on this side do not accept that. We do not know what the money is to be used for. I think there are very worthy purposes to which money could be allocated. However, the problem is that we have seen money being squandered for years. When I first came to this place, the budget was about $12 billion in total ,J''and was considered large then. Look at it now. The budget has increased tremendously over the years. So the Minister of Finance has established a record. It seems to me that we should not quickly accept that sort of thing. When it comes time to vote later today, I will be voting against this Bill.
There are all kinds of examples of squandering of money. The Government has squandered money on the PIP grants, with 93-cent dollars. We hear about the ocean oil rigs, icebreakers and all the rest; they are owned by private companies but financed with public dollars. We think that is a bad way to spend money. At the same time the Government is cutting back on the CHIP Program, the insulation program which would help people; it is squandering more and more money in furtherance of the mythical concept of petroleum self-sufficiency. It seems to me that self-sufficiency could be gained a lot more rapidly through a substitution program rather than poking more holes in the Beaufort Sea. We on this side are not happy with situations in which we have squandered piles of money.
For the next fiscal year we are going to spend $364 million on the nuclear program. Since 1974 we have been spending between $300 million and $600 million a year on the nuclear program. We do not feel that that was sensible in light of the fact that we have not sold one of those monsters since 1978. We did try to give them away to Mexico, to Korea and to Romania, for example. I think the Koreans were the only ones who got one. The grand total of what we have pumped into the nuclear program is $6 billion since its inception. In the riding
March 14, 1983

of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen), just keeping open two heavy water plants costs about $125 million a year. There is no doubt that we need employment programs in Cape Breton. If some of this money was for reasonable kinds of employment programs in Cape Breton, or any other riding, including my own, I think we could support it, but that is not what is happening.
We do not know what is going to happen with $14 billion we have no idea. We know that we would not need massive borrowing if we had an equitable tax system. Along with this monstrous borrowing authority Bill we are debating an income tax Bill that is as fat as a phone book, and we are being threatened that unless we pass that income tax Bill immediately, people will not get their refunds and will have to turn to the tax discounters.
We have a tax system that unfairly loads the bulk of the payments on the poor. This new tax Bill is going to put taxes up 27 per cent for a family of four, $125 a month. Taxes on MPs' salaries are going to be increased by 13 per cent. But for people like Ian Sinclair or Samuel Bronfman earning over $500,000 a year, taxes will drop by 17 per cent. Is that fair? If we were collecting taxes as we should in an equitable way, I do not think it would be necessary to borrow as much.
We are following the example of the United States. People with incomes under $10,000 a year in the United States pay 36 per cent of the total taxes. That is terrible. People under the poverty line pay the bulk of the taxes in the United States. I thought taxation should have been based on the ability to pay. Obviously it is not in the United States, nor is it in Canada. This new tax Bill makes the situation in Canada more inequitable, and this is not acceptable.
If we had a stimulative kind of budget, if this Bill had come forward in a package with a budget, then we could have examined it, we would know what we were getting and what we are going to spend our money on. I think it is very important to look at how we are spending our money. I would like to quote from the lead editorial of the Toronto Star of March 4, 1983. The Toronto Star is hardly a socialist rag. It might have some political leaning but I do not think it is to the NDP, or to the Conservatives either. The Conservatives have The Globe and Mail. I do not know what paper supports our Party unless it is the Toronto Sun.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Yes, don't forget Hawkes-not Jim, but Prime Minister Hawkes of Australia.
Getting back to the point I was attempting to make before I was heckled and rudely interrupted by catcalls, mainly from my friends, I would like to make this point. The study of Professor Bellan indicates that if the City of Winnipeg, or any other city which has all the facilities to put people to work, was given $1 million for public works, immediately the Government would get back $140,000 in revenue from taxes on materials used, etc., and save $380,000 on Unemployment Insurance and welfare. Therefore, of the $1 million, the net spending would be half a million. At $25,000 a job, $1 million would create 40 jobs. A billion dollars would create 40,000 jobs. If you take this borrowing authority of $19 billion, in fact take it up to $20 billion across Canada, 20 times 40,000 would be 800,000 at $25,000 per job. The borrowing authority of $14 billion and $5 billion could be used to create almost a million jobs in Canada.
If we knew that we were borrowing the money for those 20 communities across Canada, I would be happy because the choice is between spending money on welfare and Unemployment Insurance and public works. It is eminently sensible to do this when municipalities are all set up to do that kind of work. The unemployed are all ready to go. Parks, sewers, sidewalks and roads could be built immediately. If you pump that kind of dough into that rather than pumping it into losers like Candu reactors, we would have a much better chance of coming out of this recession.
People are scared. They are not buying. That is what is wrong. There is all kinds of money in the banks, but there is no confidence. If there were this opportunity of that kind of spinoff for jobs, my Party would support this Bill; but we will not support a blank cheque.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow my friend from Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) on this Bill. I especially appreciate the flattery he showed the Tory Party by spending so much time discussing us and the various kinds of Tories there are. I know the people in British Columbia are aware that he also is a Tory, but he is a "transitory" and will not be around after the next election!

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
It is with some difficulty that I speak on this Bill because it is easy for us to be against borrowing. I think everybody in Canada is opposed to borrowing of any kind, even though at times it is necessary to do so. We recognize that we are in extreme economic difficulties, so there is a call to do some borrowing.
One of the things that is in the Government's favour at this point is that the numbers we are talking about are so astronomical that the public has lost all sense of context of the situation we are in. To speak of borrowing $19 billion is a context which is foreign to any of us, so what we are really dealing wth escapes us.
There are some very indigenous problems with this Bill. The first is that the Government wants to borrow more than it really needs at the present time. That, I believe, is wrong in principle. I believe it is wrong for us to do it at home. It is wrong for business to do it. Most businesses understand that when times are tough, you have to hunker down, and you cut back on all of the overhead you can. One of the greatest places for overhead to exist is in interest payments, so to borrow more than you really need in a business seems to me to be counterproductive. Yet the Government is setting this example to business &rf655;-l across Canada, saying: "We need $5 billion but we want permission to borrow $19 billion, $14 billion more than we need". That, Mr. Speaker, is wrong in principle.
I believe it is also wrong politically. Convention and the law of the land require the Government to come back to Parliament for authorization every time it wants to borrow money. The Government really wants to play fast and loose with the whole process. Since the Government would need to borrow money again a few months down the road, it would like to avoid that kind of exposure in the public forum, the confrontation and the publicity of that extra borrowing. It wants to skirt around the parliamentary process by borrowing a lump sum now far in excess of what it really needs, and that, I believe, is wrong politically and wrong in term of the whole parliamentary process.
Second, this borrowing authority flies in the face of any kind of known or demonstrated ability on the part of the Government to forecast its own expenditures. My colleague, the Member for Mission-Port Moody has already indicated that the Government wants to be able to borrow this money without telling us exactly how it is going to spend it, and that is wrong. But it has not been able to forecast its own expenditures either, or its own indebtedness.
I believe all Hon. Members here realize-and the public has caught on to the fact-that in the last four presentations of either economic statements or disclosures, the size of the public debt has already doubled. The expected public debt has doubled and is now around $27.2 billion, whereas earlier it was supposed to be no more than $10 billion or 12 billion. If the Government has no more administrative ability than that, it seems to me we are compounding the problem by giving the Government authority to borrow $ 14 billion more than it needs
at the present time. If it is going to borrow money, that money has to be accounted for.
The third reason that this Bill is wrong, Mr. Speaker, is the reason I have already alluded to, and that is that the Government is introducing this Bill without disclosing how it wishes to spend the money. In the Blue Book Estimates we have seen some indications of what the Government's plans are, and it is startling to see what the Government is beginning to do.
I would like to dovetail this with my next point, which is that the Government is introducing a double standard regarding what it requires of the country and what it wants to demonstrate for itself. The Government says the country ought to be guided by the six-and-five principle, but when it comes to itself, that principle should not apply.
I would like to put on record exactly what the Government is doing in terms of its own Departments. When it comes to managerial expansion, the management boom, take note of the percentage increase over the previous year for management levels, that is the number of management personnel and the increase in salaries. In the Depatment of National Revenue the percentage increase in management costs is 209 per cent for 1983-84, whereas in 1982-83 it was only 5 per cent. In the Department of Communications the percentage increase is 157 per cent, whereas in the previous year there was a drop of 6 per cent. In Supply and Services the percentage increase is 134 per cent and in the previous year it was 20 per cent. In Transport the percentage increase is 127 per cent, whereas last year it was 1 per cent. In CEIC the percentage was 124 per cent, whereas last year it was 1 per cent. In Public Works the percentage increase is 102 per cent and last year it was 5 per cent.
Just to illustrate more specifically, Mr. Speaker, in the Solicitor General's Department the Regional Directors for the Correctional Services have historically been called just that, "Regional Directors", and they were in charge of the regional offices. Just before the six and five program was introduced, all of a sudden they were no longer "Regional Directors". Now they are Deputy Commissioners. That change of title, Mr. Speaker, means a new salary scale. So whereas the country is asked to stay with six and five, the upper levels of the bureaucracy find all kinds of ways of getting around it so they can get the kind of increases they want.
As the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody indicated, at the lower levels they have to hunker down, but at the upper levels the spending carries on. These are conditions, Mr. Speaker, which the Government would condemn in private industry. When a client who is strapped for money and needs some operating cash, comes to the Government's own bank, the Federal Business Development Bank, that bank has the client come back and back and back again to give it further documentation on how the money is planned to be spent, for further justification for the need to borrow that money. The poor client who is strapped for cash and wondering how he is going to exist has to set another appointment to justify to the bank why he needs the money. The adage holds true: if you can prove you do not need the money, you can get it.
March 14, 1983

The Government has not proven that it is going to spend the money wisely, yet it is coming to us, Mr. Speaker, for authority to borrow $19 billion. It seems to me, if we have a situation where 25 per cent to 28 per cent of all Government revenues are being spent to pay the interest on its indebtedness, we have bad Government and we have had management. Therefore, I cannot see how the Government can justify borrowing $14 billion more, which is over $1 billion a month more than it really has need for at this present time. I come back to the point I raised several times in the House, and that is when the Government floated a bond to the Canadian public just over a year ago, it paid excessive interest rates. Six months later it was proved that it was paying far too much. The Government itself paid over $2 billion more in interest charges than it needed to. In the process, it deprived private enterprise of doing the job it wanted to do in order to get the kind of cash it needed to do its job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue on with the point which was raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). I believe he gave a very good example to point out why we are opposed to this kind of legislation. The Government is essentially asking to borrow $19 billion with two very simple pieces of paper. It is not giving us any idea how it intends to spend that money, and we are concerned. We are concerned for precisely the reason stated by my colleague in his concluding remarks.
The Government set interest rates for the Canadian Savings Bond issue at over 19 per cent in the fall of 1981. Subsequently, it was shown that that interest rate was way, way too high. It has been estimated it cost the Government somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2 billion, and that is only part of it. The other part of it is that it forced the whole interest rate structure to go higher than it should have. We in the Opposition are not irresponsible. We realize that the Government has to borrow money because it has to meet its commitments. But we believe that in a parliamentary system, if there is to be any proper accountability, the Government should come before us with a budget so we can have both sides of the story. We realize that the Government has to borrow money, there is no question about that, but at the same time we believe there should be a budget so we can see how it intends to spend that money.
When Governments become as large as they are, and if we essentially combine the spending of different levels of Government, whether it be federal, provincial, municipal or civic, and take it as a percentage of the total disposable income of Canadians, we find that very close to 50 per cent of all money earned by average Canadians is taken away in the form of taxation and is spent by one level of Government or another. That is a tremendous amount of money. When we agree to essentially a form of taxation-and this Bill is a taxation Bill as much as it is a borrowing Bill because the Government will have to tax to come up with the money to repay this loan-at
Borrowing Authority
least we should have some say in, or some indication of, what the Government intends to do with the money.
To put the matter in perspective, every time the Government talks about $1 billion, it is talking about roughly $40 per capita. If we take $19 billion, do the arithmetic and relate it to a family of four in the country, it means that this Bill will account for something like $3,000 in borrowing for each family of four. This is a tremendous amount of money.
As I said, we are not opposed to this Bill because we are irresponsible; we are opposed because we are responsible. It would be a much happier day if we could stand in the House and pass a Bill authorizing the Government to borrow $1 billion or $2 billion, which would indicate that it is running its financial affairs properly. It would be no problem. It would be a much happier day for all of us in Opposition if we could say something kind about how the Government is managing its affairs.
As I said, $19 billion amounts to over $3,000 for the average family of four, and we are given no indication of what the Government intends to do with it. We have seen the Estimates but they do not really mean a lot in terms of the direction in which the Government intends to take the country as far as fiscal and monetary management is concerned. We are expected to rise and blanketly approve that amount of expenditure on behalf of our constituents. I submit it would be totally irresponsible of us to give the Government that kind of blank cheque. This is why we are opposed to this kind of spending.
Also we are opposed to it because when we have Government spending of this magnitude it becomes very, very inflationary. I could give all kinds of statistics on that, but generally it is agreed that beyond a certain level Government deficits-and the reason the figure is so high is because the Government is running a large deficit-get to be very inflationary. Those are some of the problems we have with this kind of Bill.
There is another problem about which I would like to talk. I noticed that in the speech of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) two or three weeks ago he spent some time talking about the definition of inflation. The classical definition of inflation is simply too much money chasing too few goods. The Government has chosen to attack inflation from the money side, from the spending side, by trying to cut down on the number of dollars which are supposedly chasing the too few goods. It has chosen to go with the accepted or classical definition of inflation.
I submit that we need to attack the other side and do something about increasing production. When we get to the level of the very high interest rates which the Government has used to control the amount of spending, it simply hurts people who are trying to be productive. In my mind it hurts one of the most important sectors of the country, and that is the farming community. We are seeing the results of this today. I understand there are people here from the Farm Survival Association and that there will be a demonstration on the Hill this

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
afternoon. This is a result of some of the foolish policies the Government has pursued for the last two or three years.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Stupid policies.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Yes, stupid. I could call them worse, but certainly the policies of the Government are misguided. This is why we are again into a situation where the Government has to borrow a ridiculous amount of money and tells us nothing about how it will be spent. We should have a budget and be able to see that the Government is pursuing some productive policies.
Some people are concerned about a Private Member's Bill, Bill C-653 in the name of the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson), concerning the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. This House will not approve something which will cause more problems for the banks and force the banks to cut back on lending. We are responsible people, we will not do anything like that. In lieu of the Government doing anything, we should be sitting down and talking about the situation. Let us get the Bill before us, remove the obviously objectionable parts of it and get it to Committee so that we can have a discussion on it. In many ways it is almost irresponsible of the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex to put forward a Bill for political purposes which contains some measures that in the banks' mind will cause additional problems for farmers.
I have met with some of the people from the Farm Survival Association. I have talked with people in my own constituency. In fact, that is the major thing I do when I go home. I have not talked to one of them who has asked for a hand-out. There may be some who are doing that, but the majority are asking for some time to put their financial houses and farms in order. Over a period of two or three years, if they can have some time and add the additional interest which they are forgoing now on to the length of their mortgage, they may be able to survive and be productive. We are talking about 10 per cent of the farmers in Canada. Perhaps that does not sound like a lot, but if you were one of the 10 per cent, Mr. Speaker, it would be very, very important to you. Even with the 10 per cent figure we are looking at approximately 25,000 farmers. This is a lot of people facing financial problems.
For us to do nothing in the House, to say simply that there is no problem and that it will go away if we ignore it, is totally irresponsible. We require a budget so that we could see, for instance, that the Government was addressing some of the excess taxation-at least I feel it is excess taxation-on farm fuels, or that it was addressing some of the problems of farmers who will be attempting to obtain a line of credit this spring. If we could see some relief, say a minimum $20,000 line of credit, it would give farmers some hope that the Government cared about them or was at least willing to listen to their problems. For us to do nothing is totally irresponsible.
I want to put to rest any of the fears of the banking institutions if we agree to put Bill C-653 into committee and, by implication, will pass something which will cause more problems. We will not do that. We will try to do something to help farmers in conjunction with all the financial institutions to get
ourselves out of the mess which the stupid Government has helped get us into. If we are to do something in the House, that is the kind of attitude that we on this side will bring to that kind of legislation.
I have a few suggestions for the Government concerning what it could include in a budget if it were really serious about helping farmers. As I said, it could include a relief from the approximately 60 cents of gasoline tax which the federal Government takes from every gallon of fuel used to produce food. Presently there is a 7-cent per gallon tax refund. I think it is stupid to collect it and then refund it. The first step would be simply not to collect it. That would help immediately as far as cash flow is concerned, and it would presumably cut down on some of the Government bureaucracy needed to administer it. That is a very straightforward, common-sense idea. Unfortunately, the more common sense one shows the Government, the less inclined it is to listen.
Second, the Government could simply lower the level of taxation it collects. I do not think there would be anything wrong with that. What sense does it make to try to set the level of taxation so high that everyone is driven out of business? If we do that, there is no tax to collect in the First instance. If the Government lowered the level of taxation and helped people in business, it seems to me that would be good business practice.
I see Mr. Speaker sitting on the edge of his chair, ready to shut me down. I suggest, in conclusion, that the Government take a serious look at the Western Grain Stabilization Fund and adjust the formula so that there could be a payout this year as quickly as possible. There is about $600 million in that Fund. I see nothing wrong with adjusting the formula so that at least a portion of that money is paid out to farmers to give them some money to help them get their crops in the ground, to continue to be productive citizens and to pay taxes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to spend a few minutes talking about how the Government goes about planning its financial affairs. Individuals and businesses usually plan their economic affairs on an annual basis according to a rational and proper procedure. This may involve estimating the anticipated income, then calculating the fixed expenditures. The difference between the two figures, if a surplus, is available for discretionary spending. If there is not a surplus, however, then the business or family must borrow the additional funds that are necessary to meet their needs, bearing in mind that the debt will have to be paid off in the future. That kind of procedure is used by individuals, families and businesses because it makes sense. It is logical to anyone who thinks about it.
What does the Liberal Government of Canada do? It asks us for authority to borrow $19 billion. That is more that was spent by Government at the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first came into office. It does not think that we need to know why the funds are required or what the estimate of spending and revenues is. We are not permitted to know these
March 14, 1983

things but are just asked to give authority to the Government to borrow the money. And we know that the sheep behind the Treasury benches will say "Aye, sir, aye" and give that authority.
Then we are told it is an estimate of now much the Government is going to spend. But we are not told the truth, Mr. Speaker. What a ridiculous situation that is. At the end of February we are given an estimate of spending for the year in the Main Estimates. That spending will commence about the end of March and by the end of June the House will have the opportunity to pronounce on whether the Government is authorized to spend that money. But by that time, Mr. Speaker, it will have spent one third of the amount-before the House has given permission. That kind of absurdity arises because it can count on the sheep behind the Treasury benches to say. "I will not think about it-aye, sir, aye".
Finally, we might get a so-called budget, which is the revenue side of the whole budgetary picture. It was promised for early this year, then before April 1 and now we are told it will be some time in April-who knows, it may come in May or it may come in June. Indeed, we may never get one because we are still dealing with the taxation Bill of a budget presented a year and a half ago.
Let me contrast this with the situation in the United States. On February 1 the legislators in the United States are presented with the Government's estimate of spending and taxes- both sides of the equation. They have an opportunity to study it, to recommend changes and to make changes. They have until the end of October to deal with the legislation and pass it for the commencement of the fiscal year. They would not dream of allowing the Government to spend money before the legislators authorize it.
We have a different system in Canada. We have responsible Ministries. Is it true that our Ministers and our Government have more discretionary authority than the United States Cabinet Ministers. Our Ministers are always responsible to this House and therefore that extra discretion is justified.
How does this House hold Ministers responsible for what they do? What mechanism do we have to give truth to what I consider to be a lie-the suggestion that there is ministerial responsibility in this House? No such thing exists, Mr. Speaker. The "Coalgate" affair really demonstrates that the responsibilities of the Ministers will extend only as far as they allow them. When the sheep on the backbenches are ready to say "Aye, sir, aye", no matter how atrocious the behaviour of a Minister, how can the House hold a Minister responsible?
Apologists, such as the Michael Pitfields of the world, will say that there is at least disclosure, and ultimately at the ballot box the people can decide. Perhaps there is not ongoing ministerial responsibility but at least every four or Five years we have a chance to re-elect or defeat the dictatorship.
But how much disclosure is there really? How much do we know about Government spending and taxing plans? I humbly suggest we know very little. I should like to deal with two
Borrowing Authority
examples of how the Government is flim-flamming this House on the spending Estimates this year.
First of all, there is the usual lock-up where the media is secluded with high-priced officials from Treasury Board who brief them. Members of Parliament are not allowed in that lock-up lest we get to them and give the lie to many of the statements made by the high-priced Treasury Board people.
We are told that this year's spending is 9.6 per cent higher than last year's. That is flim-flam, Mr. Speaker, because it compared the Main Estimates to the total Estimates of last year. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) claimed that there is a reserve for any Supplementary Estimates that come in this year. They also claimed there was a reserve last year but that turned out to be false. So why should we believe the Government now, when it compares apples and oranges? Anyone in the media who published that 9.6 per cent Figure should be chastened by their superiors for publishing falsehoods.
The other thing the Government has done this year is to reduce the PIP grants by $642 million. The Government is using practices that are contrary to accepted accounting principles and it should be chastened for this. Indeed, it should be taken to court and punished for this flim-flamming and for publishing false accounts. A private company most certainly would be punished for the same sort of thing.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has put before us a Bill asking for authority to borrow another $19 billion without giving us any reason other than to say that the Government is faced with higher than expected expenditures and lower than anticipated revenues.
A more detailed explanation of the "why" behind these expenditures and revenue figures has had to come from this side of the House, since the Government, for obvious reasons, is loth to draw attention to its legacy of wasteful and inefficient programs, profligate spending, wildly miscalculated estimates and projections, blatant mismanagement and staggering federal debt-the interest alone on which now eats up 20 per cent of our total revenues.
Attention hardly need be drawn to the unemployment crisis which accounts for an ever greater proportion both of expenditures and lost revenues-because there is scarcely a family in the country in which one or more members have not faced the spectre of prolonged unemployment. But we are dealing with a Government that is evidently bankrupt not only of resources but of ideas and, it seems, of the very will to govern, which is a very different thing from the will to retain power. It will print and borrow money in prodigious quantities, but it seems unable to make that money work for Canadians by creating jobs, enhancing productivity and generating prosperity.
As a result, the discouragement of the unemployed, the underemployed, the disadvantaged, the aged, the poor, and

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
yes, even those who are more fortunate, is turning into cynicism and despair. And this, surely, is the most devastating consequence of all in the present malaise-the erosion of a sense of hope and the loss of belief in the future of this great nation.
It is partly for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that I would like my remarks today to be particularly positive and constructive. I would like, briefly, to make suggestions and pose imaginative possibilities. I would like to go beyond the "why" of our present economic woes to consider some "what ifs" with respect to our economic future.
I would like to suggest at the outset that what we need most in this country is not merely more money but a new imagination. We need to concern ourselves primarily not with the astronomical abstraction of $5 billion, $19 billion or $26 billion, but with the 23 million Canadians whom we represent and who are not abstractions at all but individuals with faces, names, families, talents, needs and aspirations.
I wonder what would happen in this country if the potential of every individual was being challenged, not by sermons about restraint but by genuine incentives to productive and creative contributions to our economy?
What if internship and on-the-job training programs were extended and fortified, job retraining projects were enhanced and adult education enriched? What if our most promising graduates and research professionals were assured of finding employment in their own fields? What if the innovation and initiative of the entrepreneur were being rewarded rather than stifled by regulations and restrictions? What if it were profitable for individuals to develop new products and new companies, to establish new businesses and initiate new projects?
At the corporate level, what if businesses starting up in slow growth areas were provided with a 150 per cent tax credit to cover capital and labour costs for the first three years of operation? I am not talking here about an outright grant; I am speaking rather of allowing a newly-established or expanding firm to apply these expenses against future income tax payable. This would provide the investor with an opportunity to recover his investment plus 50 per cent and his labour costs for the first three years plus 50 per cent. At the same time it would create a new corporate taxpayer and ensure the creation of badly needed jobs, all without taking a cent from the federal treasury.
With respect to our most venerable and well established firms, what could we be doing to enhance productivity and prevent obsolescence in an age of rapidly changing technology? If we allow ourselves to be passed by in the rapid march of technology, our competitive edge in even our most traditionally successful fields will be lost. If, on the other hand, Canadian firms are enabled, with Government incentives, to improve technology and undertake appropriate research and development, they can begin to make the necessary long-term adjustments that will ensure us of both success in tomorrow's world marketplace and a more stable and productive domestic economy.
At the regional level, research and development is a particularly critical factor. Problems of regional disparity can never
be dealt with effectively if we fail to maximize the particular strengths and potential of each region. Atlantic Canada, for example, has one of the largest fisheries in the world and an extraordinary potential for development in fishing related industries. Yet participation is modest in the manufacture of deck hardware, propulsion machinery, fishing gear, processing equipment and navigational devices. Our own shipbuilding industry cannot at present compete effectively with subsidized foreign suppliers. What if this unrealized potential began to be tapped? Could "One of the largest fisheries" become also "one of the most productive fisheries" in the world?
As we have been reminded in recent weeks, regional initiatives can be particularly vulnerable to political patronage and otherwise inappropriate interventions. If our regional potential is continually subverted by such interference, by oversights, delays or failures of imagination, the effects will be enormously consequential for all Canadians. If, on the other hand, regional disparities can be largely overcome and regional economies rejuvenated, the need for transfer payments will diminish and ultimately vanish altogether, alleviating a great federal financial burden.
At the national level in terms of both domestic and foreign trade, we desperately need new policies and new strategies. What if, for example, Canada established a series of free trade zones in port cities? Such zones have been created and operate successfully in selected American ports under the U.S. DISC program. Imported components are assembled in American assembly plants using American technology, according to American specifications, providing good American jobs, and then exported world-wide. I would like to suggest that we consider pilot projects of this kind in Saint John, Halifax and Vancouver.
On other fronts, are our strengths in high technology and communications being used to their greatest advantage? Are our innovations in computer assisted-design and computer assisted-manufacturing being sufficiently utilized? Are the possible civilian uses of the Canadair pilotless reconnaissance aircraft for ice patrols, forest protection and research, etc., being explored?
More efficient trading nations have reached the apex of their success not by accident but by planning. We need, as Canadians, so by planning effectively, assessing the priority import needs of emerging nations and bending every effort to making Canadian projects available at competitive prices both at home and abroad. We need a Government that will be hospitable to business, industry and investment, that will provide incentives for efficient management and operations, that will, above all, restore a climate of confidence, trust and optimism in this country.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would like to submit that the "what ifs" I have posed here today represent not mere wishful thinking but common-sense alternatives and possible roads out of the never-never-land into which the present Government has led us.
March 14, 1983

It has been estimated that if only half the unused capacity of Canada and the United States were put to work-15 per cent of the available plants and equipment, 6 per cent of the officially unemployed and 5 per cent of the unofficially unemployed-an additional $900 billion worth of output would be forthcoming. That would not only wipe out budgetary debts in Canada and the U.S., but eliminate also the cumulative international debts of the developing nations.
Having considered some of the "what ifs" the obvious next question is why not? I believe the Government owes the Canadian people an answer to that question before it receives authority to add another penny, let alone $19 billion, to the gaping maw of the federal Treasury.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you have been tilting for a minute. Thank you for just tilting and allowing me to finish my speech.

Mr. Speaker, I do appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate, if only to bring a little balance to some of the comments made by Members opposite.
It is very difficult to understand just where the New Democratic Party stands. We were castigated for the deficit. First we were told that it was all right, that we needed a bigger deficit which would give us more stimulus in the country. Overnight there was a reversal of that position and the Leader of the NDP said that the deficit was big enough, to leave it and to work within these particular guidelines. Then Mr. McDermott got to the Leader of the NDP. He had to rechew the cabbage, reinstituting the original position of the NDP that it does not care about the precise size of the deficit as long as everyone is back to work. It is a very easy position for them to sell but it does make one wonder just where the New Democratic Party stands on this particular issue.
When the Official Opposition talk about our asking for a blank cheque, I must question whether they have done their homework. The Estimates were tabled only recently. We saw page after page of Ways and Means detailing how the Government proposes to spend its money in the upcoming year. All of the figures are there in considerable detail. As well, specific descriptions are given of how the various Departments will use their increases, why they are taking a particular action or where particular cutbacks are taking place. If the Opposition were really doing their homework, they would be more specific about where cuts should take place and give us some indication what they are talking about. They simply nit-pick about the budget, which anyone can do on a budget in the billions of dollars. Individuals can do that with their own budget. Even when an individual has a budget in the thousands of dollars, it is still easy to nit-pick and indicate areas where too much is being spent.
The Official Opposition have not narrowed their criticism to say, for example, that the expenditure for National Defence should be cut by $2 billion or $4 billion, or even that it should be enhanced. They have not said that we should cut down on
Borrowing Authority
the amount being paid to Provinces with respect to health and welfare, for instance. Instead, they take the popular position and say that the federal Government is arbitrarily telling the Provinces that, while they will receive transfer payments, they will be made according to a regimen. However, this is done so that we may plan our particular budget.
We hear the Opposition tell us to cut down on expenses but not to cut down on transfers to the Provinces. The fact that the federal Government spends significantly more than the Province of Ontario for post-secondary education in that Province does not seem to worry the Official Opposition. They are quite content to have that procedure continue, but I think there should be more accountability for the money the federal Government gives to the Provinces in the area of education which is under provincial jurisdiction. The federal Government is paying significantly more than the Province on the postsecondary level.
No one is asking for a blank cheque. One does not have to be an economist to realize that we are going through a recession. There are 12,000 unemployed workers in Sudbury. Those people were paying taxes when they were employed. Thanks to Unemployment Insurance, they are collecting benefits. They are collecting those benefits because far-sighted Liberals in earlier Governments saw fit to put an Unemployment Insurance Program in place that would be beneficial to those people who are unemployed. However, they are not paying income tax at the present time and, of course, that significant revenue is lost to the federal Government. This same situation is true for several industries in the country.
It may be simple to blame the federal Government for the fact that these people are unemployed, but it is not the Government that sets the price for nickel in the international market. We do not set the price for many of the items that our basic industries must sell, obviously at a profit. If the prices set in the international market are such that the industries cannot operate at a profit, significant changes must be made. This cannot be blamed on the federal Government. It is the responsibility of the federal Government, however, to devise forms of assistance that will be in place so that those people facing that dilemma can be helped while riding the wave of recession.
Unemployment Insurance is not a welfare program. It is a program for which our people have paid a significant premium. Many pay that premium in the hope that they will never have to collect it. But now that they do have to collect Unemployment Insurance, they are grateful that that program is in place. The money for that program is not simply placed into a bank account. It is used immediately for the people who need it.
A community such as Sudbury very heavily depends on the pay cheques of the Sudbury miner. Therefore, it is very dependent on the Unemployment Insurance money that is going into that city on a weekly basis. It is helping the small businessman in that community through a very difficult time. While many Sudbury miners will be called back to work on

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
April 1, it is the Government's responsibility to help those workers through the difficult times they are experiencing.
I was interested to hear the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) singing the praises of the American system of government. He seemed to be very much in accord with the idea that a budget had to be passed by a certain date. There is a time allocation procedure in the U.S. Congress for the passing of fiscal legislation.
If the Hon. Member has visited Britain, he will know that in the Mother of Parliaments at Westminster there is an understanding with the Official Opposition that once a party is elected and becomes the government, it has the right to have its legislation passed through the House. The Opposition has the right to give legislation some ventilation-the word I heard most often-to bills and spend as much time dealing with particular bills as it deems necessary. The Opposition sets its own priorities as to which bills they will attack and those for which they will allow speedy passage.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise with my colleagues on this side of the House and speak in opposition to Bill C-143. While it may sound repetitious to mention $19 billion, let Canadians know that this Bill breaks a record. This Bill will result in a debt that will be the largest in our history. It is the largest borrowing Bill in Canadian history.
Bill C-143 has been introduced with little justification in relation to its expenditures. It will mortgage the future of our children and their children's future as well. More importantly, the headlines of today's paper say that the graduates of this year are asking "What future?" Who can blame them?
I heard the comments of the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) dealing with the Estimates. We all know that very shortly those Estimates will be deemed to have been passed. As we consider the big spenders on the other side of the House, we must remember that just four months or so ago, in October, the Government stated that the deficit of $22.2 billion would be sufficient to see it through this fiscal year. Now, just over four months later, it wants an additional $5 billion to continue through the fiscal year which is in front of us. An additional $14 billion is requested for the fiscal year 1983-84.
The Minister, with the endorsement of the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton, says "Trust us". When have we heard this phrase before? The people of Canada simply turn their backs. Where is the credibility? Where is the honesty? Where is the confidence?
I would like to quote the words of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen). Just a few months ago, he emphatically said:
I would not expect the House to act upon an additional request for borrowing authority without providing it with detailed information on the economic situation and the implications of that situation on the Government's fiscal situation. I do not think it would be appropriate to ask the House for additional borrowing authority until I have laid out in some detail an update on both the economic situation and the fiscal situation, and I certainly will be doing that before I would come back to the House for additional borrowing authority.
Those words of the Deputy Prime Minister could not be clearer, yet we hear the Minister's successor asking for an additional $19 billion for borrowing purposes. Where are the explanations? How can the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) so freely ignore the words of the Deputy Prime Minister? Is it because the Deputy Prime Minister no longer has credibility?
March 14, 1983

Can he defy those words because he, too, has lost the confidence and trust of the people of Canada?
Not only do we in the Opposition want to know why the Bill is being introduced, but we also feel that Parliament has a right and a duty to question how and where the money will be spent. It is our parliamentary responsibility to the people of Canada to prevent a majority Government, the backbench Members of which simply sit on their hands, from continuing to borrow and borrow and spend as no other Government has spent before. This Parliament must be more than a rubber stamp.
I ask on behalf of my constituents of St. Catharines, will the Bill provide jobs for our automobile industry workers or our shipbuilders when those in the manufacturing industry of the Province of Ontario look for job incentives and opportunities?
What is at issue here does not particularly concern the request for $5 billion for the current fiscal year; we at least have some idea why that request is being made. It involves two totally disastrous budgets and a catastrophic energy program. The $5 billion is part and parcel of the Government's inept management of the economy of the country.
However, what is the forecast for the future? The $14 billion for the fiscal year 1983-84 is another matter altogether. Canadians do not want to see a repeat of last year's performance. They want some direction, leadership, and common sense, and to start the year off by borrowing $14 billion to spend on who knows what is simply an indication of following the forecasts of years gone by, the era of the big spenders.
According to the most up-to-date information available from Revenue Canada, the average taxpayer in the City of St. Catharines earns $20,000 a year. That same taxpayer pays over $3,000 in federal taxes. The Government has already borrowed $2,100 against the name of every taxpayer of that city. Now, through this borrowing measure, it proposes to add another debt of $500 to each and every one of them. Having borrowed $2,100 per taxpayer, it will follow that up with increased carrying charges. Assuming interest of 10 per cent, it would amount to a further $210 per taxpayer in the riding of St. Catharines. The passage of this legislation will add a still further $50, increasing the tax payable by each one of those by $2,100 plus $260. My constituents cannot afford that amount, nor can the people of Canada.
As I pointed out, the average taxpayer in St. Catharines now pays $3,000 a year in federal taxes. An increase of $260 would represent a hike of almost 9 per cent in extra carrying charges only. It does not take into account the Estimates to which reference was made earlier. It does not take into account additional federal spending which might be indicated in this fiscal year, nor a budget, the contents of which we know not. I point out that we in St. Catharines pay, as a whole, $165 million a year in federal taxes. A 9 per cent hike on that sum would almost amount to an additional $15 million.
Last month St. Catharines and Niagara had the highest urban unemployment rate in the land. How can we stimulate
Borrowing Authority
the local economy and set people to work again by increasing tax measures, by increasing the burden on the present populace and future generations who will live therein? I suggest to Your Honour that it is not necessary to bankrupt the Treasury and mortgage those future generations of taxpayers. It is not necessary to build Windsor on the back of St. Catharines. Difficult times require decisions and the Government must make decisions.
The only sector of our economy which is not practising restraint and setting priorities of spending is the federal Government. Day in and day out, we are treated to new examples of Government spending by Governments which are oblivious to the strains being placed on the shoulders and backs of the taxpayers. Over $1 million has been spent on newspaper ads to tell us just how close we are to energy self-sufficiency.
In the last 15 years, Government spending has risen at an unprecedented rate and much of it has been since the present Government was elected in February of 1980. Relating those years to fiscal 1979-80, spending has increased by 59 per cent, a sad commentary on those who say that the Government is practising restaint. For every $4 it spends, it must borrow $1, and borrowed money must still be paid for. The cost of interest on the debt of the last fiscal year was forecast at $16.7 billion, the equivalent of one revenue dollar in three. It is no wonder that our young Canadians look with concern to their future. It is no wonder that we Canadians, the people of this country, are concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are signalling that my allotted time has almost expired. I will conclude in just a moment.
The taxpayers of St. Catharines cannot afford to pay more. An examination, as the amendment before us proposes, is the only reasonable approach to fiscal control and expenditure. Alternatively, it leads those of us on this side of the House with no alternative but to oppose this astronomical borrowing Bill, Bill C-143, and that is what we intend to do.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to follow the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). In completing his remarks, he said that his Party has no alternative but to oppose the present measure before us, the measure to increase the borrowing authority. Of course, that is the role of the Opposition in the House of Commons. However, I think what we are increasingly seeing in this Parliament is that the Opposition is going beyond its role of opposing and criticizing and is trying to impede the orderly flow of legislation through Parliament.
My colleague from Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) touched on this a moment ago when he mentioned that in other jurisdictions, in the United States Congress and in the Westminster Parliament, there is an inherent recognition of the right of the Opposition to criticize, to vote against particular measures and

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
draw public attention to the weaknesses in proposed legislation; but that in the final analysis the majority of members in a legislative body, in this case the Canadian House of Commons, must carry the day.
We have seen in this Parliament, for example on the Constitution resolution and the energy legislation of last year, a continual thrust on the part of the Official Opposition to try to frustrate the will of the majority of Members in this House after legitimate and full debate has taken place. That is perhaps one of the greatest weaknesses of this Parliament, and I would hope when the Conservative Party resolves its leadership question that the first item of business for its new leader, or the present one if he is confirmed, is to take a more responsible approach to Parliament. If the Official Opposition ever hopes to form a Government in this country, I think that Canadians will expect them to behave in a responsible manner. Certainly their conduct throughout this Parliament has given very little reason for Canadians to believe that the Conservative Party truly does respect the workings of Parliament.
I want to talk about the substance of the matter for a few minutes because I believe that the Government is fully justified, after nearly 80 Hon. Members have spoken on this measure, in bringing in time allocation to get this Bill through. The borrowing requirement of the Government of Canada covers an urgent need. A lot of rhetoric has flown from the other side about why the Government requires this money. There is no doubt that the present Government deficit is fully defensible.
I sometimes wonder, when I hear Hon. Members, especially from the Official Opposition, criticize the deficit, if they really have been talking to some of their constituents when they make these criticisms. 1 represent what could be described as an inner-city constituency in Metropolitan Toronto and I know as much of the full effects of the recession as any Member in this House. I am sure that the Hon. Member for St. Catharines must go home every weekend and talk to his constituents because he represents an area where there is a lot of heavy manufacturing industry which has been hard hit by unemployment. I am sure his constituents are not telling him to come to Ottawa and oppose to ridiculous lengths the requirement for borrowing these funds, because the deficit has performed a great service to Canadians in the past year.
When we look at the projected deficit for this year, the high twenties of billions of dollars, we have to recognize the central factor that most of it is cyclical in nature. In other words, the deficit has increased due to the demand placed upon the Government Treasury by the recession. People have not been working; therefore Unemployment Insurance payments have been higher. People have not been paying taxes because they are not working; therefore Government revenues have declined. It is a matter of pure and simple economics.
The Government is faced with two choices. One is to continue to provide for those generous social welfare programs that the Opposition embraced in the good times-and here I think is the real crux of a commitment of a Member of Parliament in this House to social reform-ten or fifteen years ago when
