subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it comes as no surprise to my colleagues on both sides of the House when I say that in rising to speak on this Bill I make no pretence of being either a political historian or a political scientist. However, without any trepidation I am going to attempt to put into perspective what I believe to be the attitudes of Canadians generally, because those attitudes, in my view, have a very direct bearing on Bill C-143 wherein the Government seeks authority to borrow another $19 billion.
Historically in my view, Canadians have had an attitude which, if expressed, would be something like this: "We may disagree with what you, our Government, are doing but at least we believe that you know what you are doing". There was a residual confidence built up over 100 years in the federal Government, particularly in its economic program. It was built up despite from time to time anger, even outrage, strong opposition to some measures, particularly budgetary measures, and despite from time to time the adverse effect that these measures would have on certain groups or sectors of Canadian society. Despite all of this, Canadians continued to say: "We may be very mad or angry at you, we oppose this particular Bill or budget, but you should know what you are doing".
In my view, this contributed to our stability. Stability, progress and expansion flowed from this residual confidence. Given this history, attitude and confidence, where do we find ourselves as we wait for the Government's 1983 budget? Firstly and obviously, we are in a severe recession. This is
Borrowing Authority
partly because of international, world-wide conditions and partly because of domestic conditions in which our record compared to those of other industrialized countries is dismal, to say the least.
Canadians cannot blame outsiders, foreign governments and international conditions for our problems, because that simply is not true. Because of both the international scene and Government incompetence, we are suffering from tragic unemployment and its resultant loss of productivity and human misery. We continue to suffer interest rates that are much higher than any economist believes they should be. We continue to suffer the erosion of our lifestyle because of inflation, particularly those least able to protect themselves. We continue to suffer the results of Government spending, as emphasized in this Bill. All of these, except the human misery factor, are measureable.
Second, and in addition to these hard economic facts, we have a situation that is not measureable in absolute terms but which may be equally as serious. For lack of a better term, I call it the psychological factor because, unhappily, Canadians have lost confidence in their Government. Despite our tradition and history, Canadians are now saying that for the first time they not only disagree with what people in Ottawa are doing, but are convinced these people do not know what they are doing.
Evidence of this is everywhere, in my riding as in all ridings across the country, particularly in small business and farming where those able to expand and progress, those not at the mercy of high interest rates, turn to Government bonds at 19'/2 per cent instead of expanding their small business or increasing their productivity as farmers. That was the test of lack of confidence. If I were to agree, as I do, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who says that the private sector is the engine of recovery, I say to the Government that if you believe that, why are you trying to spend your way into prosperity? It will not work. Increased Government spending has not reduced unemployment.
What happened to the traditional residual confidence of Canadians in their Government and, following that, in themselves and their communities? I do not think there was any one incident; it was gradual. Government spending and borrowing increases in 1968 caused a deficit of $497 million. That has increased to likely $30 billion in 1983, an increase of 5,936 per cent in the Government deficit. That has contributed to the erosion of confidence.
Government spending out of control, the Turner budgets of the early seventies, when I first came to this House, contributed to the erosion of confidence. The lack of Government accountability, as indicated in Auditor General report after report, the National Energy Program, conceived in stubbornness, born in ignorance and implemented with disastrous results, contributed to the erosion of confidence. Certainly the MacEachen budgets were the straws that broke the camel's back.
All of these combined to achieve a destruction of the traditional confidence of Canadians. In this situation, incidents

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
which Hon. Members opposite think are relatively minor become major irritants. The $800 to Donald Macdonald does not have a substantial effect on the budget, but imagine the salt it poured into the open wounds of Canadians from coast to coast. Not so minor in nature was the Coalgate or Gillespie affair, a million dollar payment for a very dubious project.
We wonder why Canadians are outraged, why they have no confidence and why they are saying those in Canada do not know what they are doing. In our current atmosphere, Canadians will seize on these issues. They will do things that are completely out of character, such as a penny auction in my riding and a person arrested on a hunger strike-completely out of character in the Canadian context.
Do not be surprised because desperate measures will be taken in desperate circumstances. None of these, however, destroys confidence as much as Bill C-143, a request to borrow $19 billion without any indication as to Government financial forecasts. No control, no accountability, no disclosure and the Government leaps into the money market to compete with small-businessmen and farmers for loans. The Government presents the largest borrowing bill in Canadian history without telling the country where we are headed.
We are to wait for a budget before we find out the Government's economic forecast and strategy. The Government says: "Trust us, have confidence in us". That flies in the face of every economic and psychological factor that exists in this country in March, 1983.
It is natural that I should oppose. That is not my sole function as a Member of the Opposition, but it is part of my function. It is natural that I should oppose Government measures, particularly one that I take so seriously. That is not important. The fact that Opposition Members rise in opposition to a $19 billion borrowing Bill not the significant factor. Rather, it is what my constituents and Canadians everywhere think. Those constituents are saying that rather than expanding their small business, rather than becoming more productive on their farms, rather than hiring additional help or building up inventories in order to produce more, should they leave their money invested in Canada Bonds? Not one job is created thereby. That is what Canadians are thinking in the face of the $19 billion borrowing Bill. Until those Canadians have a change in attitude and the only factor in that change is an increase, not a decrease and erosion, of confidence, all the Government spending in the world will not turn that situation around.
In summary, and I see my time is almost up, in addition to trying to survive the hard economic facts, Canadians are being smothered by a psychological barrier which has resulted from a lack of confidence in their Government, a lack of confidence in themselves, their future and that of their families, and even a lack of confidence in the community in which historically they have thrived and prospered. The Government's response to that psychological situation is to come to this House and say: "Trust us, have confidence in us and give us the authority to borrow $19 billion". On behalf of my constituents and on behalf of Canadians, to that request I say no.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I join with my colleagues on this side in speaking in opposition to this Bill, which requests authority to borrow $19 billion and places an unprecedented burden on Canadian taxpayers in terms of repayment.
As my colleagues have pointed out, this Bill is unique in character. It is based completely on our trust and confidence in the Government to manage our economy. It is unprecedented in the sense that the Government has not come before us with a budget or spending program to indicate how this money will be spent. As I said when I spoke on this Bill last week, the crime of taxation is not so much in the taking as it is in the way the money is being spent. This Government will take most of this money to continue its insidious drive toward total control of our economy.
I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was kidding last week when he said that for a Minister to leave his Cabinet and not be working with Government in some way would pretty well deprive him of his livelihood. He would have to stand on Sparks Street with a tin can and beg for money. I do not think he was kidding because it would be very difficult today for anyone to go into business without being a partner of Government.
That really is the root of the problem which this Government has gotten itself into. It would not matter very much what kind of forecasts the Government would lay before us because its forecasting has been totally out of whack, completely wrong. Government does not have a very good track record. We are still dealing with three prior budgets during which spending has gone from $11 billion to $24 billion. Therefore, it really does not matter much what kind of a forecast the Government would lay before the House. But the question arises, and it is a simple one: If you go to your bank to borrow a large amount of money, surely the banker would first want to know what you need the money for, and second, what you have got to offer as collateral.
Incidentally, to put $1 billion into proper perspective, it has been said it is a stack of brand-new $1 bills 85 miles high. The average person cannot comprehend $19 billion. I know it would take $2 billion to put in place an income security system which would be totally financed and sound actuarially. To take away any anxiety of our senior citizens in terms of retirement income would take $2 billion, and this Government wants $19 billion.
I do not know whether there are some retired Liberals out there who need another $1 million each. I do not know if it is the Government's intention to buy more service stations. I do not know what the Government wants to do with this money. I know there is nothing in any of the programs or legislation before the House right now which would even give me the least bit of confidence that this Government knows what it should do in terms of turning around the economy and creating jobs. It has a new commission now, the Macdonald Commission. A retired Minister, who receives $800 a day, is now out around
March 14, 1983

the country trying to figure out what the Government should do with the economy. We in the Opposition are being criticized for being critical. That is our role as the Official Opposition, but we have nothing to criticize. All we know is the Government's insatiable appetite for power. Karl Marx always said that the cultural and economic theories of a society are merely the reflection of the vested interests of the ruling class. In his time, of course, taxes were low, profits were high and the capitalists were the ruling class. Today profits are low and taxes are high, and since taxes are the income of bureaucrats in Government, it can only be reasoned that the Government and its bureaucrats are the new ruling class. They are the new oppressors, the bureaucrats and the Government. They are the new capitalists, and it is not so much capitalism in the material sense but capitalism in the sense of the raw exercise of power, the uncontrolled exercise of power. They are the new capitalists.
How is the economy reacting to this unrestrained appetite, this kind of unrestrained Government spending? The corporations are reacting in strange ways. The corporations over the last 10 years have not done what corporations normally do in terms of expanding their business. They have indulged themselves in this exercise which is now known as "paper entrepreneurship". Instead of building a new plant, developing a new product and making a contribution to the economy in terms of creating new jobs, they find companies on the stock market whose assets are undervalued and they gobble them up. That is what I call corporate cannibalism. They do that because they are nervous about Government. They have to compete with Government. The banks are competing with Government. All of this does not create one new job or do anything to ease unemployment or inflation. All it does is put a demand on the money market, putting all the capital pools into one big bowl, splashing them around and handing them out to those in the privileged position of raw power as it is exercised by this Government.
The tragedy of this unbridled borrowing as well, Mr. Speaker, is that there is not enough capital in our own country. Federal, provincial and municipal Governments are borrowing much of that money abroad. In other words, the 25 cents of every dollar which every Canadian taxpayer gives to the Government is spent on interest, which is in turn spent abroad somewhere else.
One can turn on the television set every night and hear this criticism of the American economy: "Reaganomics has failed. Massive deficits will create new pressures on the money supply and interest rates." Well, if we look at the American deficit we see it is $80 billion, but that is two and a half times less than what the Canadian deficit is in real terms, and the Americans, of course, borrow from their own people, from their own institutions. We go abroad, however, to America and borrow the money there. Twenty-five cents of every dollar is paid to some institution in the United States, in Switzerland or in the
Arab States. That is the tragedy; the money does not even stay in our own economy. Our own banks cannot even build up any capital pools to lend money to small business. And what have the banks done in reaction to this kind of raw power? Have they made an effort to build pools in order to lend to small business, to medium-sized business, and in doing so create new jobs? Of course not. They have lent money to Dome Petroleum, to Chrysler, to Mexico and to Guatemala, because it is just as easy for them, Mr. Speaker, to service a billion dollar loan to a foreign country, which is guaranteed by the Government, as it is to service a $30,000 loan to a small business. That is the tragedy. The trend is set right there and, sir, we must stop it if we want to save our economic freedom in this country and, in so doing, our personal freedom.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT MAJOR CONCERN OF POPULATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT MAJOR CONCERN OF POPULATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when asked to identify the major problem in the country today, Canadians placed the jobless rate far ahead of inflation, or any other issue, as their major concern. Sixty-five per cent of those surveyed by Gallup said the Government should be giving much greater attention to trying to reduce unemployment.
Compare that clearly stated concern of the Canadian people with the response of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) when questioned about the latest unemployment figures last Friday. With 1.6 million Canadians unemployed, he dismissed their concern with an attitude of "All is well, a recovery is under way, " or "All will be well, just pass the Income Tax Act," or "No need to worry, just wait for my budget."
This is not the first time the Liberal Government has shown its contempt for the views of Canadians, nor the first time that it has been out of step with what Canadians consider to be the number one priority. But in the face of such massive evidence that Canadians believe unemployment must be dealt with immediately, that joblessness is hitting hard, not only at the unemployed but at their dependants as well, surely the Government has an obligation to bring in job creation measures now, and not wait until some will-of-the-wisp budget to do so.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I was watching the American PBS channel from Vermont this weekend, I could not help comparing their system to ours. The American Government is spending $85 million for a population of 230 million. We pay ten times that amount, namely, $850 million for ten times fewer people. subtopic: CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO IMPROVEMENT OF LIVING CONDITIONS IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO IMPROVEMENT OF LIVING CONDITIONS IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since 1976, the second Monday in March has been designated Commonwealth Day following a proposal by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at a meeting of heads of State in Kingston, Jamaica. While many of its members, including Canada, have evolved in the constitutional sense, the Commonwealth has remained a privileged forum for forty-seven countries, nearly one quarter of the world's population. Colonialism has gradually given way to political consultation and cooperation among peoples.

Commonwealth Day should be used primarily for educational purposes, so that developed and developing member nations could learn about the Commonwealth and life in other countries.
On this day Commonwealth countries around the world are marking the occasion with enthusiasm in a wide range of activities. We in Canada should value the many forms of association with the Governments and people of the 47 countries of this world-wide association representing one-quarter of the world's population.

Canadians have made a tremendous contribution towards improving living conditions in many developing countries that are fellow members of the Commonwealth, through common institutions or bilateral aid programs.

On this day, then, it behooves us to commemorate our longest continuous multilateral association with other countries, to remind ourselves of the value of that association and the contribution Canada can make politically and economically to its further evolution and well-being.

maintopic: STUDY OF HOSPITAL WORKERS USING VIDEO DISPLAY TERMINALS
STUDY OF HOSPITAL WORKERS USING VIDEO DISPLAY TERMINALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently a study was completed by H. D. Sharma, a professor from the University of Waterloo, based on 75 video display terminal operators working in British Columbia hospitals. Sharma found an abnormally low rate of pregnancies among the women of child-bearing age and, of the 14 VDT operators who became pregnant over the past year, ten had miscarriages or gave birth to babies with defects. This is only one of many studies with similar results.
A Government task force report on microelectronics made recommendations which could reduce the number of birth complications and other physical problems that are associated with VDTs. At first the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) endorsed these recommendations, and said that they conveyed a sense of urgency. Now he is backing away from the need to legislate health and safety protection for VDT operators, in response to the lobbying of employer groups. The Minister of Labour must find the courage to act immediately on behalf of the workers and their children who need the protection of Canadian law.

IMPORTANCE TO ECONOMY-CALL FOR GASOLINE TAX REDUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House and of the Minister responsible the fact that there is a very simple, practical and inexpensive way in which the Government can move to assist the revival of the economy, by directing its support to the industry which ranks, at least in Ontario, as the second largest generator of jobs. Furthermore, it is geographically so dispersed that, more than any other employer, it can generate a widespread positive leverage throughout the economy. Of course I am speaking of the tourist industry.
In Ontario alone last year it generated $7.4 billion in revenues and created a ripple effect generating $12.6 billion. That represents big money in a country which is trying to encourage an economic recovery. Yet, on a bilateral basis with
the United States alone, in 1981 Canada ran a deficit on tourist account of $1 billion. Surely that is due in large measure to the fact that gasoline, which ultimately fuels all tourism, is 10 cents a litre or, in terms that our would-be tourists can understand, 45 cents a gallon more expensive here than across the border where the world price is in effect. A simple cut in this federal grab would cause a beneficial effect to ripple all the way through the domestic Canadian economy, and I recommend this course to the Minister.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice in the absence of the Prime Minister. On the eve of the historic First Minister's Conference on Aboriginal Rights, the Government of Canada has left its position unclear on a basic question. I refer to the need to entrench within the Constitution itself a requirement that a certain number of First Ministers' meetings take place over a prescribed and limited period of time to deal with the important question of defining aboriginal rights. Will the Minister take this opportunity to commit the Government to fighting for such an entrenchment, a desire that is requested by virtually every native group in the country?
Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice and Attorney
General of Canada): Madam Speaker, I think it is fair to say that the commitment of the kind my hon. friend seeks should probably come at the conference itself. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Considering that the latest Statistics Canada figures reveal that 209,000 of the 450,000 unemployed Quebecers are in the Greater Montreal region, and that in all likelihood many of those idle workers are about to exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits, will the Minister try to convince his Cabinet colleagues to ensure that half of the projects within the federal scope of the NEED Program will go to the Greater Montreal region?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT HALF OF NEED PROGRAM FUNDS BE ALLOCATED TO MONTREAL METROPOLITAN REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to the question I want to point out that one of the particular attractions of the NEED Program is its ability to target in on those areas where the demand and concern with regard to unemployment are at their highest level. Contrary to the somewhat callous approach taken by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, who would totally deny any assistance to the people in his own Province, as evidenced by the kind of proposal he was making, our ability through the NEED Program is to allocate the money where benefits have been exhausted and where the unemployment rate is highest. On that basis, we are working to ensure that the Montreal region in the Province of Quebec is particularly served by our programs.
I think it would be important for the House to know that we do not wish to follow the precedent set by the previous Government, which cancelled all job creation programs. Nothing would be done for any Canadians, at any time, anywhere, if the Conservatives were in power.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. I would like to know whether the Minister of Transport is aware that the report of the 1965 Industrial Inquiry into CNR Run-throughs, which is known as the Freedman Report, made this observation, and I quote:
-there is a Government obligation towards communities whose existence or stability is threatened by a run-through or its consequences.
The CNR is proposing once again to run through the community of Nakina, that is, not have any crew changes there. It says that $1.2 million will be saved per year. The community, at the same time, is going to lose $1.5 million in a reduced tax base. I ask the Minister of Transport what will this big federal Government do to help a small northern Ontario community whose stability is threatened at the very moment in its history when it is starting to get on its feet and enjoy some of the services that most other Canadian communities have?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: NAKINA RUN-THROUGH PROPOSAL

Madam Speaker, the Canadian National has followed the practice in these matters, in this instance and in the past, and the run-through has been negotiated by the railway and agreed to by the workers, or their union. There is another aspect that I recognize which has to do with the town itself. In this instance I will associate myself with the Member in representations that he will want to make to other Departments in order to find out if there are ways and means to help the community.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are entering the final hours of another closure motion, this one on a $19 billion borrowing Bill. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) has just risen in his place to advise us of time allocation on the income tax Bill, a Bill two and one half inches thick, containing hundreds of Clauses which will adversely affect the lives of every man, woman and child in this country. He has announced closure on that Bill. That is an insult to this House, an insult to the very purpose of Parliament, which is for the people of this nation to be able to control executive authority. It is an insult to all ordinary Canadians.
Every Canadian should be as outraged as I am that this Government can run this nation into such huge debt and then, in a device to get out of it, say we need more Government, more Liberal Government. We are not going to put up with that. Anyone who voted Liberal in the last election has had a knife driven into his back, and it is being twisted more every day. Canadians will not make that mistake again, I can assure you of that.
This is the seventeenth or eighteenth time the Government has announced closure. Where are we as a nation? We are in deep trouble. Unemployment is high. Farmers have been put in jail. A young farmer is now starving himself to death. There are tens of thousands of farmers on the verge of tipping under. As history has taught us so many times before, when you let agriculture go down you destroy the family farm. We have not

March 14, 1983

yet seen the tip of the iceberg as to the problem that the people in the cities and the 1.6 million unemployed are going to have as a result of destroying our farmers. Just as sure as the sun will come up tomorrow morning, people in the cities will rue the day they voted Liberal and put in a gang which for 15 years has been causing this country to hemorrhage and bleed as if we were some Third World country.
Let us not forget where we were in 1968. We had balanced budgets. We had a national debt which was just a drop in the bucket. Yet we had a post-secondary education system which was superb. We had five or six jobs being generated for every graduate who came out of university. We had a medicare system which was the best in the world. We had Old Age Security, hospital insurance and Family Allowances. This country was strong and we were racing up the mountain as a real power to be in the future. Then we put in a Liberal Government under a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is still running this country, and, Mr. Speaker, things have gone downhill ever since.
Where do we find ourselves today? We have a budget deficit which is $30 billion a year. We find a national debt which is $200 billion-plus when you add in all the Crown corporations, and that is just simply a way of doing indirectly what the Government knows it cannot do directly. The post-secondary education system is in a shambles. Hospital insurance is breaking down. The medicare system is in a shambles, and people are feeling insecure. The Old Age Security system for our senior citizens has been destroyed so that our senior citizens know that if they are forced to retire today, within five years their money will be worth only half what it was, as compared to 1968 when a person could retire and with a rate of inflation of 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent it would be 25 years before their money would be half the value, and by that time they would probably be gone. In short, Mr. Speaker, we could cope with a couple of per cent inflation but we cannot cope with 20 per cent and we cannot cope with 20 per cent interest rates.
That is what is destroying our country. We not only have our hospital insurance in difficulty but we have our postsecondary education system in difficulty as well, so that our university graduates do not have any jobs. How can that possibly be, Mr. Speaker? We have 24 million people, one half of 1 per cent of the world's population, a drop in the bucket. We are sitting on the resources of half a continent yet our university graduates cannot get jobs. Our high school graduates cannot get jobs. How can that be, Mr. Speaker?
I can tell the House how it can be. When you put too much power into the hands of too few people, you are heading for trouble. The Liberal Cabinet, 36 men and women, with a small bureaucracy around them at the senior levels, believe they can run this country better than the millions of ordinary Canadians and, Mr. Speaker, they are driving us into the ground.
We are not going to tolerate this because the lesson we learned in our western democracy is that when the king made decisions affecting the capital of the nation, the nation never
got ahead. When that capital was broken up into millions and millions of individual pieces, and an individual would give their whole life, effort and energy making decisions about that capital, it created wealth in the western world and raised the poor of our world to a much higher level than even the kings and queens in the old days. That is what economic capitalism will do, Mr. Speaker. But this Liberal Government does not believe it because it wants to make the decisions.
It goes beyond economics, Mr. Speaker. They will soon want to control our political life. They will then want to control our social life. In Western Canada we have millions and millions of square miles and acres of land all divided off into one-mile squares which fit together perfectly. Every mile you go west you hit a road. Every two miles North you hit a road. Millions of acres were surveyed that way. This Government is now going to convert this land into metric measurement so that 160 acres has now become 64.75 hectares. Every mile becomes 1.6 kilometres. That is the illogical outflow of a socialist Government which wants to control everything. It wants to remake mankind in its own image, its great socialist image.
I believe we are in this jam today simply because the Government wants us to be here. It believes if it can bring everyone to their knees then people are going to call for more Government, and it is going to be there to say: "We'll save you. Forget the fact that we caused the problem, ladies and gentlemen, but we will save you." That is not going to work, Mr. Speaker, because Canadians en masse are going to see that it is a circular argument; that if you call upon that same Government to create more Government, we are going to be in even deeper trouble. I believe that is what the polls are showing today. Canadians recognize that there are a group of men and women over there who really believe they can run this whole country, while practical experience shows they cannot. In the next election they will be wiped off the map and no one will be happier than myself, and perhaps even you, Mr. Speaker, because I know you are a wise man.
How is it that the youth of this country does not have a future? As I said earlier, we have all the resources. Surely it is because of the so-called "Canadianization program", which you and I know, Mr. Speaker, having looked at the fine print, is not Canadianization at all. It is nationalization. Again, we have under nationalization this concentration of decisionmaking by this group of men and women who are not practical businessmen and women, who are not practical farmers or people out on the steet who really know what it is like. These men and women have had great education and often ended up at the London School of Economics as their finishing school, but it does not mean a tinker's damn because they do not know what it is like to meet a payroll. That is the difference between someone who is a good Government politician as compared to those guys today.
Look at the great leaders we have had before. Even C. D. Howe understood how to make wealth, Mr. Speaker, and that was by taking the strength of our resources and putting them into the hands of people who would devote their full time and
March 14, 1983

effort to it. You then get good decision-making, and if you have enough competitive systems going, then there is a constant thinning out at the bottom, but it is only of smaller corporations so that the released workers can be reabsorbed.
This gang opposite want to concentrate things into massive dimensions, and if they then fail, the result is tens and tens of thousands of people unemployed. That is not the way we should do things in this country. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that every day I am receiving more and more letters from ordinary Canadians who see the ruse, and it is a pleasure now to go out and talk to these people because they are beginning to take their sovereignty back. What Canadians must do is call each of us out as politicians and find out where we stand as individuals and what we believe their rights are economically, politically and socially. We will then have them electing the best person from each riding, Mr. Speaker, and it will not be Liberals.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before us in the House today is yet another borrowing authority Bill. It is the fourth of its kind in eight months. The others were Bill C-111 in June of 1982 which asked for $6.6 billion, Bill C-125 in July of 1982 which asked for $7 billion, and Bill C-128 in November of 1982 which asked for $4 billion. Now we are being asked for $19 billion, $5 billion of which is to be used to get through this fiscal year, the remaining $14 billion to be used as interim money for the period ending October, 1983.
Asking for this money, Mr. Speaker, without a financial statement is tantamount to writing a blank cheque for Government policy. It is hardly an approach which we could possibly endorse. While this amount of money is high relative to other requests for borrowing authority, it is not unprecedented. However, the manner in which the Government is doing it is noteworthy. Thomas Walkom of The Globe and Mail said, and I quote:
While it is not unheard of for a Government to ask for some interim borrowing authority, a $14 billion request without a budget is unprecedented.
As all members know, the borrowing authority offers Hon. Members a chance to complain about Government policies and generally the way in which the Government chooses to spend its revenues. I am sure that most members have enough information at hand to criticize how this Government spends money in the fields in which they are interested without any additional information from the Government.
I want to talk about some of the things the Government has done. We have seen it put the clamps on important social programs. We have seen it bring in the six and five program. It started by applying it to the salaries of federal public servants and those working for Crown corporations, but then it applied it to Family Allowances and old age pensions. The pensioners, the women and children of this country are being asked to bear the brunt of the present economic difficulties. These are being brought on to a large extent by the mistake in economic policies of the Government.
Borrowing Authority
Now we hear that funding to universities will be cut by the application of the six and five guidelines to the Government's contribution to university education. For the first time in a number of years enrolment in the universities has increased. That is because many young people cannot find jobs and are going back to the universities and community colleges. This is happening at a time when those institutions need more financial assistance in order to give people the kind of training that Government spokesmen say they will need in the job market in the next 10 or 20 years. There will be an increase in the emphasis on technical knowledge, computerization and microtechnology. Yet the Government has put a 6 per cent and 5 per cent limit on the increase of funding for universities.
Let me give another illustration of the stupidity of the Government, Mr. Speaker. It has abandoned the Crow rate which for years has protected Canadian farmers. It is doing this at a time when bankruptcies are at an all-time high. In February they increased 32 per cent over the same time last year. Yet the Government abandons the Crow rate and tells Canadians farmers that there will be an increase of up 500 per cent in the cost of shipping grain in the next few years. This tremendous increase will have to be absorbed by the farmers as they cannot add it to the price of the grain on the international market and expect to compete. While this is going on the Government is subsidizing the CPR, one of the largest and most profitable Canadian corporations, so that it can improve its track. As well, VIA Rail, which is supposed to move passengers, is permitted to continue in its weak state.
This Party is not opposed to a Government deficit, Mr. Speaker. We recognize that it is inevitable, particularly in a time of recession when the private sector is not expanding and investing in new facilities and techniques because it is operating at less than 70 per cent capacity. This is the time when the Government should be increasing expenditures to improve the transportation system, the environment and housing stock. We are not opposed to the Government running a deficit or borrowing, but we see no evidence of a plan or a strategy to meet the country's needs.
We are opposed to the Bill because it is obvious that the Government has abdicated its responsibility for putting an economic policy before the people. It has given responsibility for dealing with the problems of the country to the Bank of Canada to a degree that we find unacceptable. It is supposed to settle our economic policies by bringing down the rate of inflation. It has managed to do that but at the expense of everything else, particularly unemployment. There are now 1,600,000 people unemployed, the largest number ever, and the rate of unemployment is higher than at any time since the great Depression of the 1930s.
The recent Gallup poll indicates that the people of Canada believe that unemployment is the major problem facing the country today, yet the Government continues to concentrate on the supposed threat of inflation. The Government's singleminded attack on inflation has only been marginally successful but it has been a disaster for the economy. It has resulted in the largest number of people unemployed ever, 11,000 business

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
bankruptcies in the last year and a record number of farm bankruptcies. The economy is running at less than 70 per cent capacity.
While the Government is putting the clamp on social and economic programs, there are many examples of waste around. We see $100 million poured down the drain with Consolidated Computer, poorly thought out DREE programs, the Mirabel white elephant, incredibly lucrative grants to the supposedly suffering oil companies, and then there is the spectacle of deserving Liberals appointed to position after position.
The Government is continuing to clobber Canadians by raising taxes for low-income earners through deindexation and raising Unemployment Insurance premiums. Taxes are decreased for investors and upper-income earners. This is supposed to provide the engines of growth but these tactics have failed to produce any results whatsoever. The "trickle down effect" is simply not working.
While we see higher taxes for those who can least afford them, the Royal Bank, which made several hundred million dollars of profit last year, pays an effective tax rate of less than 1 per cent. It sounds strange but in fact the Royal Bank had a negative tax figure last year because it received a tax credit for over $125 million this year.
We cannot support this borrowing Bill brought forward by a Government which has no economic policy, no strategy and which is going from one disaster to another.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speeches this morning and this afternoon given by the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), the Hon. Member the Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) and now the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
There is a recurring theme in the speeches and a recurring question asked by all Hon. Members. They seem to say; "We do not know what the money is for. We do not know how the Government will spend it. How can you ask us for more money when you have not shown us how you are going to spend it?" I suggest that one requirement for becoming a Member of Parliament in this Chamber should be the ability to read. Had all speakers who preceded me learned how to read and read through the Estimates, they would have learned exactly how every penny will be spent. I refer Hon. Members who spoke before me and who will speak after me to the Estimates wherein it is spelled out very clearly and exactly how every dollar or every penny will be spent.
The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) at least admitted that there is a call to do some borrowing. He complimented the Government on that, but he said that the figures were so astronomical that the public could not comprehend them. I think the public can comprehend
them; I think it is the Hon. Member who cannot. The figures seem to be too large for his comprehension. He went on to say that this move was wrong politically. I do not know why that should worry the Official Opposition. If it is politically wrong for the Government side, then it should be politically good for the Official Oppositon. Opposition Members should be urging us to go further on this route which they claim is politically wrong. I think they are worried that it is politically sound, good and on the right track. The Hon. Member went on to say that the Government wanted to borrow this large amount without telling the public what it needed the money for. We heard this over and over again. Again I refer that gentleman to the Estimates.
The Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) said that some of the money the Government wanted should be spent on search and rescue, that if it were used toward putting youth to work for the Canadian Armed Forces, perhaps he would vote for the Bill. He went on to say that he wanted money spent on bridge pier fendering around his constituency, which are clearly a provincial jurisdiction. He wanted the federal Government to pay for them, and he wanted more money for icebreaking facilities and vessels. Also he wanted more money for fleet replacement of the Canadian Coast Guard. This is great, but he did not say where that money would come from. It is fine to say, "Give me this, give me that", but tell the public, Canadian taxpayers and the House, where the money will come from. The very things he mentioned that he wanted are listed in the Estimates. That is where the majority of the money will be going.
I invite Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party and of the Official Opposition to come to the Standing Committee on Transport tomorrow morning at 9.30 a.m. when the Minister will appear before it. Then they could question him on how these funds will be spent in the Department for which the Minister and I are responsible, the Department of Transport. I think this is a great democratic process, where every Department is held accountable to the public or the country at large through elected representatives.
Opposition speakers this morning and this afternoon were almost unanimous in asking what the Government would do with these additional funds. They suggested that perhaps some of them could be used for job creation, and then they would support the Bill. Let me remind Hon. Members opposite that we have had a great debate over the last year on the western transportation initiative. Professor Gilson was out West listening to the grassroots people, listening to all sectors of the economy so as to come up with recommendations on how we could improve the entire western transportation system. If the House were to implement his recommendations soon, they would create 375,000 person-years of work over the next decade. If Hon. Members opposite are serious about job creation, why are they not supporting the changes to the Crow rate and the western transportation initiative? If both Parties opposite are really serious about job creation, why are they not
March 14, 1983

speaking out publicly and supporting the western transportation initiative, which will create 375,000 person-years in the next decade?
Also I make very clear the long-term objectives of the Government as far as job creation is concerned, as well as its short-term goals in job creation. In my home riding, last year over 50 students obtained jobs through the Summer Canada Program. Again this year organizations are submitting applications to provide jobs for high school and university students this summer. The intention of the Program is to provide jobs only for the summer months, so that these students can earn some money to help pay their tuition fees come the fall. It is not meant to provide these students with permanent jobs; that is not the purpose of the Program. We should make clear and distinguish the difference between long-term initiatives such as the western transportation initiative and something like the Summer Canada Program or the NEED Program which will get exhaustees, people who exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits, back to work. They do not want welfare; they want to work. Mr. Speaker, they tell you and me that.
Again using my own riding as an example, I point out that on the books there is a project to provide jobs for 15 workers to work in Ontario Place, a provincially-owned complex. Another 15 workers have been provided jobs in a community centre in my riding. There are other pending projects to provide jobs on the Canadian National Exhibition grounds, getting them ready for the summer. Again, these jobs are short-term ones. We agree with that. I think everyone would agree that these people would rather work and be paid than go on welfare. I could talk about the Canadian Community Development Program, but I do not think time would allow it.
The Government has demonstrated good management and how to spend taxpayers' dollars prudently. The Opposition mentioned that we should spend more money putting young people to work through DND. We have to look at that very carefully. I was one of the Members on this side who signed a petition containing 108 signatures and making this recommendation, but I did not sign it with the intention of putting all our eggs in one basket. If it costs $25,000 to train one young Canadian in certain skills over the next two years, but through some other program we could train two or three young Canadians to learn the same skills in the same amount of time, as good managers we should ensure that we steer more money to more efficient training for young Canadians.
Another example close to my riding is the Toronto International Airport. Projections showed that in the 1980s we would need a new Terminal 3. Because of the downturn in the economy and a drop in air traffic, the projections now indicate that we will not need a new terminal until the 1990s, and we have postponed it until then. Again I think this is good management and that this is prudent spending of taxpayers' dollars.
We heard charges that we were just throwing away taxpayers' dollars foolishly. I do not think we are doing that. We have demonstrated wise spending and good management. Speaker after speaker this morning and again this afternoon said,

Mr. Speaker, when any Member on the Government side of the House can stand in support of what is in the Blue Book and what is in the borrowing Bill, he or she has not taken a look at the real world. For instance, we heard discussed today the unemployment rate in the Province of New Brunswick, which exceeds 15 per cent. We have a cabinet Minister representing the Province of New Brunswick who has stood idly by while a transfer of the DND operations is to take place from his Province. He has at no time indicated in any way that he stood behind the appeals of the Province of New Brunswick to keep that DND installation active and employing people in the Province of New Brunswick. Instead of that he has apparently acquiesced and recognizes that in 1984 the DND operation will be transferred out of perhaps one of the most highly unemployed areas of Canada. That is our Minister from New Brunswick in this Government's Cabinet.
The same Minister has taken a look at agriculture and decided that he will dilute the agricultural research by establishing a second branch in the Province of New Brunswick at the expense of personnel in other research stations in Atlantic Canada. Any knowledgeable individual not so politically biased as our present Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) would recognize that extension of the knowledge accumulated in research is very necessary in New Brunswick but that division of the research structure into a second unit would certainly give us diminution of real results of a concentrated effort taking place as it is in that Province. He has done precisely the same thing in research with respect to fisheries. We have one of the most renowned research stations in the world at St. Andrews, New Brunswick. Again, we are going to dilute that and put people in an establishment which is probably a two-hour drive from any meaningful salt water, the object of research. That is our Minister. He did not even locate that establishment in Chatham, New Brunswick. He cuddled it into his own constituency in his usual political way, not caring two hoots about what is good for New Brunswick but perhaps only considering what is good for him as a Cabinet Minister. That is the way we are represented. That, Sir, is why we oppose more borrowing for more stupid political behaviour by this Government.

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
Why did the Government not pick up the idea once promoted by the Province with respect to the development of the oil shale potential, either as a source of oil or as a source of fuel for electrical generation? Instead of that, the Member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley) pooh-poohed everything that might be practical, and he in turn was supported by our Minister of Public Works. The reason New Brunswick does not approve of the borrowing of $29 billion is that it has been ignored purely for political reasons.
In the field of agriculture we watched the impact of the change in the capital cost allowance and in the investment in capital goods allowance. In the constituency of Victoria-Madawaska it cost a farmer $12,000 more for the purchase of capital equipment in Victoria County than it cost a farmer in Madawaska County. That is within a constituency. The uneven handouts of allocation of privileges under this Government can be epitomized no better than by the division of a farming community within a particular constituency for the benefit of a particular group of people. This sort of thing cannot go on, Mr. Speaker.
During Question Period this afternoon it was mentioned that Maislin received $34 million, which money apparently was interest free and which apparently will be lost to Canadian taxpayers. We in New Brunswick in an agricultural community want to know why $34 million was poured into one firm in Montreal and $45 million had to do for all Canadian farmers under the administration of the Farm Credit Corporation. Things are pretty badly out of balance when that kind of political patronage is practised by the Government of Canada. Yes, it is a political decision and, yes, it is a bad decision for Canada.
On March 4 I raised a question about the advertising being carried out by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I raised the question again today. I believe the notice of the closing date of the summer employment programs arrived on my desk on March 1. There was no way, as the Minister suggested today, that I could disseminate that information to a rural constituency through Canada's present postal system. There was absolutely no way. I could not reach the weekly papers in my constituency. There was no media coverage. Yet the Government could spend $239 million for other advertising. My students, the young people in my riding of Carleton-Charlotte, will not have an opportunity in many instances to apply for the benefits which will come from this program.
There is more money to be made and more employment to be created by making a change in the fuel tax for agriculture, fisheries and forestry. There is more money to be made that way than in any other way in this country, particularly if this change were combined with a change in the capital cost allowance which these industries need and need very badly. Instead of that, we have unemployment almost as if by intention in the fisheries, forestry and farming sectors. We have unemployed people by the tens of thousands.
Farm income is reputed to have declined 10 per cent one year and 15 per cent the next year, and as we looked at the future of agriculture in Canada in December we saw that in the last two years we have given farmers year after year less
and less incentive and burdened them with more and more costs.
What is the consequence of all of this? I will be very repetitive because I have already stated this about three time in the House but it is worthy of statement once more. When interest rates were running wild in this country the increase in the cost of money to farmers in the potato industry exceeded the total cost of production of an acre of potatoes ten years prior to the time of the 22 per cent and 24 per cent interest rates for farmers. Yes, we are critical of this Government, Mr. Speaker. We certainly are. I had conversation last night with a couple of my grandchildren. Nothing impressed me more after I had hung up the phone than the fact that today, when I would be speaking on this Bill, what would be foremost in my mind was that I had inherited a sane, sound, sensible financial management from Government. However, after some 30 years of elected office under an irresponsible Government such as we have now, I am passing on for my grandchildren to pay, my hospital bills, my old age pension and my Canada Pension Plan. Justify that, gentlemen of the Government. I did not inherit that. My first public meeting was a school meeting in what was my school district then. The object of those taxpayers when they voted the money to rebuild a bigger and better school, was that within 20 years we must have it paid for the children of the next generation.
The object of this borrowing Bill and the Blue Book which was mentioned earlier is to live high off the hog today and let the next generation pay. The next generation will grovel in the mess left behind for them in the hog pen of this Liberal Government.
I do not know how to condemn this Government further. If I did, I think I would. We are subsidizing and subsidizing. We are subsidizing everybody but the man in the moon. We are giving no consideration and expressing no concern as to how this nation will share its social, its industrial or its economic responsibilities ten years down the road with this type of administration.
It has been pointed out what the increment will be on an annual basis as a result of borrowing today. That is what we are passing on to the next generation. Why do we not give incentives for people to invest, for people to farm, for people to fish and for people to go to work in the forests? Why are we not spending some of these moneys to rejuvenate our assets. Why are we throwing money down the gutter by way of $239 million in advertising and maybe a total of $1 billion of Crown Corporation and Government advertising? These are astounding figures to ask our grandchildren to pay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to my calculation, this is the nineteenth time in this session that the Government has used this device to cut off debate on an important piece of legislation. Today, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) rose in his place and announced
March 14, 1983

that time allocation was going to be imposed again on another matter of importance, namely a tax Bill. That will be the twentieth time in this session of Parliament that closure, or some form of it, has been evoked. This is a device that is supposed to be used very sparingly and with a great deal of discretion.
When one looks at the issues upon which time allocation was invoked, they generally dealt with financial measures such as amendments to the Income Tax Act. They are the very fundamental issues which make this institution necessary. We have seen closure invoked on 17 occasions when we were dealing with measures pertaining to the financial administration of the country. The other two occasions involving closure dealt with the question of the Constitution and the adjournment of the House.
When we review the legislative matters upon which closure was imposed, we suddently realize that this institution is no longer functioning as a parliamentary democracy. It is more like a parliamentary dictatorship. This Parliament is functioning under one Party rule and by a Government which really only represents one-half of the country.
Closure has become the rule rather than the exception. When this fact is coupled with the excessive use of Orders in Council and the implementation of such things as forced metric and the emergency planning order, the result has been a severe undermining of the institution of Parliament. It severely undermines the purpose for which the parliamentary institution was devised; to authorize the collection and expenditure of public funds on behalf of the people of Canada. In other words, the Government is to act as a trustee on the advice of the collective wisdom of this House. However, under this Government this Parliament has become nothing more than a rubberstamp. Parliament has become impotent and powerless, with no mechanism to deny the Government's frivolous, wasteful and extravagant expenditures. Parliament can only take such dramatic steps as ringing the bells or engaging in a long-term filibuster. The power of Parliament has been subverted and transferred to the hands of those who occupy the Treasury benches, supported by a group over there who follow their Party mainly for partisan purposes rather than putting the interests of the country ahead of their Party.
The views of the former Auditor General, who said in 1976 that Parliament has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse, effectively represent today an accurate reflection of where we are. It is interesting to note that the latest report of the present Auditor General highlights a similar concern. It is the fact that we have a Crown corporation proliferation in this country which really serves as a subgovernment. In effect, these Crown corporations are not accountable to the shareholders through the Parliament of Canada. Since they cannot be controlled, they continue to build empires frivolously and spend the taxpayer's money on questionable practices.
I was interested to hear the views of the Auditor General on the matter of VIA Rail when he appeared before the Public Accounts Committee. He observed that a corporation like VIA, which has extracted over $2 billion of taxpayers' dollars,

We are on a very dangerous course in this country, bearing in mind the fact that we are into that period of the year when it is tax time. People across the country will be cognizant of the fact that they are now paying their Government. What they must underline, in each of their tax considerations, is that for every amount they pay to the Government, 25 per cent will pay for interest on the accumulated federal debt.
Mr. Speaker, if you have a tax owing this year of $100, $25 would be payable simply on interest on the accumulated debt. Likewise, that means that all across the country, one-quarter of the wealth given to the Government of Canada is to pay for nothing else than interest on the accumulated debt. We are not, then, with one-quarter of our tax, building structures or ports, providing for shipbuilding industries or for the infrastructure of pipelines or assistance thereto which would create both wealth and jobs in the country. I submit that somewhere there must be some sanity which will come to the Canadian people, because if it does not come by reason of logic that we must run the country somewhat more along a business principle, it will come to us in the same way the banana republics are learning that neither can they foster economies which are weak, based on debt and borrowing, based on the fact that their resources are insufficient. Canada today would be as bankrupt as Mexico. Our debt per capita is higher than Mexico's. The only reason we are not bankrupt is that because this land is resource-rich. We are rich in forests, in minerals hardrock, in fisheries, both salt water and fresh water, and rich in agriculture.
We are a wealthy land blessed with resources. It is on that back that we have mortgage tomorrow based on the confidence of other nations. Our next generation will be in debt because the other nations know that the resources are there, in other words, the wealth is there, but the truth is that on the basis of pure economy, we are in worse economic shape than the Latin American countries. That is a despicable record for a nation which should have been doing precisely the opposite.
The truth of the matter is that if the Japanese, with their 110 million persons, took hold of these advantages of resources and talented people, they would no doubt have the wealthiest economy in the whole world today. Here we are, wanting nothing, but dropping to fortieth position according to the OECD. Japan, an island of rock with a minimum of agriculture, and the only extended list of resources being that of fish and tin, has the second highest economy in the world today. It imports all of its uranium, coal, gas and oil. In short, it imports everything. We are energy-rich. Energy being the basis of our production today, it seems to me folly that we should be in a
situation where the Japanese are able to outstrip and outproduce us. They are doing that because our Government is borrowing upon borrowing mainly for political reasons, not for reasons of industrialization.
I would like to consider the frequency with which the Government has gone back to the trough. This is the second time this year, 1983, that the Government has sought to increase its borrowing authority. In the June budget, it outlined the projected financial requirements to be $17 billion. Then, through Bill C-125 introduced in July, it sought to increase the borrowing authority from $10.2 billion to $21.2 billion, an increase of some $11 billion. The frequency with which the Government has been coming back is exemplified in Bill C-30, which received Royal Assent on July 17, through which it borrowed $12 billion and then through Bill C-59, which was given Royal Assent on April 8, 1981, allowing borrowing of another $14 billion. Then Bill C-111 was given Royal Assent on June 17, 1982, allowing the Government to borrow another $6.6 billion. Bill C-125 was given Royal Assent on August 4, 1982, allowing the Government to borrow another $11 billion. Then Bill C-128, given Royal Assent on November 8 of 1982, allowed borrowing of an additional $4 billion. Today we are debating Bill C-143, requesting that the Government borrow yet an additional $19 billion.
From 1980 to 1983, a three year period, the Government has come to Parliament to borrow some $66.6 billion. That list of borrowing upon borrowing, with the insult of this latest request without a budget in front of us, simply demonstrates, as clearly as could ever be demonstrated, the absolute incapacity of the Government to manage.
Any Canadian citizen who went to the bank to request a loan of some significant amount, be it $1,000 or $10,000, must state the purpose of the loan. A banker would ask, "What is the purpose of the loan?" If the citizen were to respond by saying, "I have no stated intentions for the money, and I just want the money", the chance of obtaining a loan would be basically nil, irrespective of the capacity of the person to pay back the loan.
The Government has asked the people of Canada to give $ 19 billion without a plan. What folly! This afternoon I wanted to make some comments concerning over-all economic policy on something which has caught the attention of the Canadian public, the Canadian media and also the House in recent weeks. I am referring to the statement by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops entitled "Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis." It was a statement made to the Government of Canada on the economic crisis which we face as a country.
In that context I would like to put on the record my own view of the theological context in which we ought to reflect on economic matters.
The God of the Bible is a God who wants to redeem the whole of human existence, our social as well as our individual life, in the end by bringing to fulfilment and completion something called the Kingdom of God. And living in harmony with this desire of God involves His followers in the world, and in the world of politics and policital choices, as an inescapable fact of being individual in the world.
What kind of world is it? Well, the original will and intention of God is for a world and for the world. Genesis tells us that God created the world and called it good. Thus, whether we find it in the form of a garden at the beginning of history or as a city at the end of history, the intention of God is for a world, a created reality which is more than the sum of its parts, an organic creation.
This is reinforced by the story of the creation of human existance per se. God creates human beings plural, male and female, in His own image. Like God, humans are personal and free to enter into relationship with each other. This is the intention of God for human life, that we enter into fellowship with Him and with each other, that we enjoy each other's company. Relation is the primary intention of human existence, relation in love, that is, but relation is also the primary structure of our existence. That is why all economic systems which ask us to perceive ourselves as rugged individuals, acting apart from the needs of the community and acting apart from the needs of others, are so much falsehood. Human beings are never without God and they are never without each other. They can only pretend that they are. The law of our being is the law of love, represented and demonstrated in the life, death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, the man for others. Christ, being a unique and special event in the life of the world and the life of God, is the means through which God has revealed what it means to be fully human and through which He has revealed Himself, that is to say His own solidarity with human

suffering and the pain of the world and the power of His love over the power of death.
Sin has its origins in human will and responsibility, the misuse of our God-given freedom by which we rebel against relation as the law of our being and try to set ourselves up as God, wanting to live a self-created and independent life, denying our relationship with God, denying our relationship with neighbours and denying our relationship with the rest of creation. I am speaking now of the way we treat our environment.
The incarnation is not the incarnation of something radically other, but the coming of God into the life and history of a world in which He is already Creator, already indwelling principle, already ultimate reality. Thus the truth of the Gospel conforms to the deepest truth of our existence. Thus we are encountered by Christ not only in His life, death and victory over death, but in the ongoing life of our sisters and brothers in human history and, more particularly, in the life and needs of the hungry, the poor and the oppressed, the least of them, as Jesus put it.
So if we follow this view which sees the primary religious axis as that between God and the world, then the Church is not a sacred island in the profane ocean of humanity gathering the select few for the heavenly dispensation. The Church is different from the rest of the world only in so far as, and when, it lives human existence more fully as a result of hearing the Gospel. Its task, like that of Israel before it, is to bear witness to the truth of our relationship to each other and to God, to tell the world the truth about itself.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking about the context in which we make economic decisions, the context in which this Government ought to plan the way the Canadian economy is run, and I think my remarks are relevant. If they are irrelevant, then we are in a sorry state indeed. If we cannot, in the context of the most general kind of economic motion that we have before us, make these kinds of over-all reflections, then where indeed could we do this kind of reflecting?
It is the responsibility of the Church to tell the world the truth about itself. The Church exists for the sake of the world. The Lordship of Jesus is lordship over the world. The life of the Church is acknowledging and living from this lordship and being instrumental to God's purposes for the world. So the Church is not an end in itself. It exists to continue the work of its Lord to help save the world, not to save individuals only, but to save the world. Not to condemn it or to help men out of it, like the Gnostics, but to save the world.
Once we have concluded that the world and its redemption is the proper focus of faithful Christian activity, we must look to the prophetic tradition in the Bible for guidance. It is here that we find a long record of protests against religion that

March 14, 1983

exalted the eternal at the expense of the temporal, the transcendent at the expense of the imminent, the vertical at the expense of the horizontal, individual piety at the expense of justice and the life of God at the expense of the life of the world. Christians must realize that we can only be in the world, even if we are not of it, if we are actually willing to be participants in history, to make choices. Standing back from the fray is not an option, no matter how much piety accompanies the standing back.
The Bishops are to be commended for speaking out, for speaking out that way is part and parcel of the Christian life collectively as the Church and individually as Christians.
If we want to act in and for the world, as God would have his image-bearers act, then we must ask ourselves what kind of choices, what kind of sides is God reported to have taken in the Biblical record. The inescapable answer to such a question is that God did take sides and that the choices he made, the sides he took, were invariably on the side of the poor, the needy, the vulnerable, and the oppressed. The continuity with and fulfilment of this bias on the part of God, because God does have a bias, in and by Christ is stated most eloquently and clearly in the Magnificat of Mary (Luke 1:46-55) where the arrival of the Lord of History is praised and welcomed as the scattering of the proud, the putting down of the mighty, the exalting of those of low degree, the filling of the hungry, and the sending of rich away empty.
God is creator, judge and redeemer. He is the judge of the oppressor, and deliverer of the oppressed. Judgment and deliverance are in a sense interchangeable in the Biblical tradition, both semantically and conceptually, depending on what is needed and by whom at any particular point in history. Both have their origins in the steadfast, loving rule of God, who wills to humanize and redeem the oppressor by breaking the prideful domination of others and to humanize the oppressed by liberating them from bondage.
The Church cannot just say that war is bad but some wars are necessary. Rather, it must say: participate in this particular war or do not participate in it. The Church cannot just say that it is wrong for people to starve, but then say nothing definite about what form a solution might take. What I am saying is that it is the responsibility of all those who would act out of a particular religious point of view to be concrete. There is absolutely nothing wrong with being concrete. In fact, it is only by being concrete that we have a hope of being right, that we have a hope of saying the word which is needed in any particular point in history.
So I repudiate the criticisms of all those who have criticized the Bishops on the basis that they were too concrete. It is only by being concrete that they have lived up to their responsibilities.
