speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to join in this discussion today. I had an opportunity last week to talk about the various points of view put forward by the Opposition.
I would like to put forward today in a more positive way my views about Government borrowing. I recall very clearly being asked my views during the last election campaign. In particular, I remember a discussion I had with the Mississauga newspaper. Each candidate in that campaign was asked his or her view about the deficit and Government borrowing. I replied that I felt Government borrowing to be a legitimate financial tool for the federal Government, that I am not afraid of using this tool. I do not see taxes and spending cuts as the only alternatives to financial crises. I see Government borrowing as an equally important tool for Governments to use.
I was reminded of this point of view today in an article in The Toronto Star by Professor Ruben Bellan, who is at St. John's College at the University of Manitoba, the economics department. Professor Bellan says that when we look at attempts to cut the deficit to get rid of Government borrowing, we get a paradox. I quote as follows from Professor Bellan's article in today's paper:
A corresponding paradox may attach to attempts by a federal government to reduce its budget deficit. To achieve such a reduction the government reduces its spending, raises the rates of taxes already being levied, introduces new forms of taxation.
The effect of its spending reductions is to put people out of work: Government employees lose their jobs, as do persons employed by firms from whom the government now buys less. Increase in rates of taxation and the imposition of new taxes have the same effect.
In short, Professor Bellan has pointed out that severe tax increases and severe cuts in Government spending tend to accelerate a recession rather than answer the recession. I agree with his point of view. I believe that Government borrowing is a way that Government can use to cushion ordinary Canadians against the blows of a recession like the one we are currently experiencing.
We heard some interesting comments in the House in the last couple of speeches. I think the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) spoke from the heart when he said we had to aim our economic policies at human misery, the most vulnerable and most needy in society. That was a laudable comment. Equally, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) discussed the extremes in the other direction, cautioning us against too much borrowing and too much spending. There is a traditional middle of the road between those two positions. It is possible for a Government to borrow responsibly and cushion its people against a recession. That is what we are doing now. I would like to point out that our borrowing is as a result of transfers to ordinary people, businesses and other levels of Government. That is the major part of our spending, the major source of financial requirements.
I would like to point out some very interesting testimony in the Finance Committee last week. One of our officials noted that if we add up all the deficits and all the surpluses of all the Provinces in this country, we actually have a $300 million surplus, not a deficit. The Provinces are in a surplus position. The federal Government carries the weight of borrowing, not the municipalities and the Provinces. It is our borrowing that is being transferred to the Provinces and other Governments,
March 14, 1983

which enables them to run their schools, hospitals, medical care, transfers to people, welfare, and social programs. That is the kind of action we have to take. We have to recognize that there are people in need who must have this cushion underneath them during tough times.
The Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) accused the Government of encouraging people to live high off the hog. Despite my affection for the Hon. Member, I regret that I must reject that point of view. I do not think our children would thank us if we passed along to them a devastated economy, and that is what would occur if the federal Government did not take the kind of affirmative action it has taken.
Our children will not necessarily appreciate the borrowing we are going through, but they will see it as far more preferable to a devastated economy. They will recognize, as I recognize now about previous people who have borrowed, that the borrowing spread out difficulties over the years, that we are able to offer the economy a little less of a blow now because we are borrowing against our future. That is acceptable. It is fine as long as it is done in a responsible fashion and we demonstrate that we can repay this borrowing at some future date.
As well, I reject the argument that we are comparable in this regard to poorer countries. Poorer countries by definition have a smaller capacity to repay such a loan. Therefore, it is a political red herring to drag in countries in Latin America and around the world that have lower standards of living and lower resources at their command.
I remind Hon. Members that in the June budget the Government emphasized the policy of a reallocation. We did not bring in huge new spending programs. Instead, we trimmed our sails in one area in order to finance expansion in other areas. We did that with purpose. We felt that the federal Government should be responsible. Therefore, we priorized our spending areas more carefully, trimmed a bit off and spent the saving. As a result, we have had $3,000 home grants that have gone right to the heart of the industry and revitalized that industry. We have railroad rehabilitation programs that are not only building up a vital infrastructure, but stimulating otherwise depressed industries. We were able to spend money to help out on unemployment insurance. We did not simply go to already depressed employers or distressed workers and ask them to bear the whole load.
We put a bit extra in. The upshot has been a higher deficit, but it has been a deficit that is affordable. We need only look at the recent experience in the -money markets to show that interest rates are coming down, that we are not crowding out the private sector, others who want to borrow.
In summary, I believe that our deficit is an important cushion for all Canadians. I believe we are the major stimulus in the economy at the present time. Without us, our economy would be flat and very desperate. Finally, I believe that our policy of reallocation and careful priorizing of our spending is paying off.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that whenever the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) speaks, rather than offering positive proposals as to what this Government is doing, he simply comments on what other Members of this House are saying. That exemplifies exactly what this Government is doing. Rather than act, it simply talks.

In the short time since the last election, this Government has increased the Canadian debt by some $90 billion. We now have before us Bill C-143. The Government wishes to have the authority to borrow an additional $19 billion without giving this House any type of commitment as to whether this money is going, without showing any economic restraints or any concrete economic policy, and we in this Party are in opposition to the irresponsible approach of our Liberal friends opposite.
I believe it is important that all of us, as Members of Parliament, reflect upon what our thoughts were when we first came to this Chamber and what prompted our involvement in politics. My reason was quite straightforward when 1 decided to involve myself in the political process in that I totally disagreed with the economic management of my Liberal friends opposite. In the close to nine years that I have been a Member of the House of Commons, that irresponsibility has grown. When we look at what they have offered to the Canadian people we see a depressed economy, one of the more depressed economies since the Depression itself.
During my short participation in this debate, I would like to review, on a very personal basis, what we in this Party are going to do about it, and why I as an individual also sought the presidency of our national association. I want to do everything within my power, Mr. Speaker, to return to the Canadian people the hope and opportunity which this country once had and no longer has under the Liberal Government opposite. I ask Hon. Members of this Chamber, and all Canadians, where did those bright hopes of the early 1980s go? When we went into this new decade, our hopes were great for this country of ours. There were a number of megaprojects which were to come on stream, but because of the inaction of our friends opposite some 10,000 jobs were lost in just the energy sector itself. I remember at one time, Mr. Speaker, that to live dangerously was at one's choosing rather than because of a Liberal Government policy.
Even though there is much that we as an Opposition can criticize as to what this Government is doing, I have found in my travels throughout this country that the Canadian people are tired of what I call "old time politics". These are politics whereby the Opposition criticized what our friends in the Liberal Government were doing. Canadians are now looking to us, the Conservative Party, to offer constructive proposals to cure the economic malaise which this Government has brought us into.

I would like to review with you a brief five-point program which we would implement in the event that we were the Government, and which we will implement after the next general election. We will reduce the Government budgetary deficit, Mr. Speaker, and we will redirect and limit Government spending. We will simplify not only the income tax forms, but also the Income Tax Act under which we function, to encourage again risk-taking investment especially as it relates to the small business sector. That is how this Government has destroyed the economic activity in this nation.
One might ask, Mr. Speaker, what we as a Party are going to do to restore a climate of confidence in this nation of ours. I would like to refer to the budget that we introduced in 1979. That budget, Mr. Speaker, squarely confronted the economic difficulties with which this nation was faced, and it proposed solutions based on sound economic management. There were policies which offered encouragement to the private investment community and yet provided protection for those who were disadvantaged in this society. Our budget contained measures which placed women in a position of equality with men so far as family enterprises are concerned. We introduced an energy tax credit to assist lower and middle income earners in Canada to meet the higher energy costs. We had our mortgage and property tax credit scheme. We had measures to help specifically the small business sector as it related to the high interest rate, which would have effectively cut interest rates in half. We have a Government which wishes to do the same thing to the agricultural sector. We have legislation before this House called Canagrex which wants to give full and total control to the Government over the agricultural sector. We on this side of the House have a responsibility to the Canadian people to offer hope and faith in this nation of ours once again.
Whenever I have occasion to speak in regard to Government policy, I am reminded of the time when the President of the United States addressed the two Chambers two years ago. He likened Government to a baby. He indicated it is like an alimentary canal with an appetite at one end and no sense of responsibility at the other. We, the Progressive Conservative Party, have to return that sense of responsibility to Government, and I can assure you as an individual Member of Parliament and as a Member of this Party that we are going to return responsibility and we are going to return faith and hope to this great nation of ours.
My parents immigrated a good many years ago to this country from Holland because they saw this country as the country which would hold hope not only for themselves but for their children. Mr. Speaker, Canadians are looking to us, as a Party, to restore that hope.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am glad we have that matter cleared up.
The Government is asking the House to give it authority to borrow some $19 billion to meet projected expenditures in the
March 14, 1983

coining fiscal year, without giving the House the opportunity to examine what it intends to spend the money on.
I have two concerns about how the Government proposes to spend this money. One in particular is the recent announcement that over the next fiscal year the Government intends to reduce the amount of money available for social housing. That is being done in face of the housing crisis in Metropolitan Toronto and Ontario today. It is irrational that this should be the case when we have the highest unemployment on reocord in the country today. It is well known that for every job created in housing construction, 3.5 jobs are created in spin-off industries. Housing is not only a social need, it is also a tool for major job creation.
Nearly 18,000 families are on the Ontario Housing Corporation waiting list. Cityhome in the city of Toronto requires
16.000	new units to handle its waiting list. Emergency hostels provided for transients have become permanent homes for hundreds of people who cannot find affordable accommodation. At the same time, thousands of units of affordable housing are waiting to be built in Metropolitan Toronto, but the federal and provincial Governments are forcing their delay or cancellation.
Today the Oak Street site is a vacant lot. If Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation would approve the housing subsidy under its non-profit co-operative housing program, the site would contain 149 units of housing, a small park and a daycare centre.
Non-profit co-operatives are developed by a board of directors and then run on a democratic basis by the tenants. By removing the profit component and by making units available to low income people assisted by federal and provincial rent subsidies, this development would provide affordable housing to those who need it most.
Metro Toronto has been allocated a 1983 budget of 815 coop housing units. This is a substantial drop, since the 1981 allocation was 1,300 units and the 1982 allocation was 1,100 units. Besides the Oak Street site, there are 14 sites in Metro where construction could begin if CMHC gave a financing commitment. These sites include Windward, Harbourside and Arcadia Co-op on the Harbour front, Lambton Co-op in York Borough, three Scarborough locations with over 300 units, three downtown locations, Toronto Women's Co-op in Park-dale and the North of Metro Co-op. With this many projects on hold, co-op housing developers must turn down all new proposals.
CMHC is a federal body and is the main provider of subsidies for non-profit co-operative housing. Given the enormous need for social housing and the high unemployment in our construction industry, the NDP has urged the Province to take direct action in the development of co-operative housing. Over
2.000	person years of employment could be created by Government investment in the co-op housing that is ready to be developed this year in the Metro Toronto area.
Cityhome is the City of Toronto's non-profit housing development corporation. Right now it requires 16,000 new housing units to meet its waiting list.
Borrowing Authority
The Ontario Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing allocates CMHC funding for municipal non-profit programs. In December the Province transferred 172 units from the 1982 allocation to the 1983 allocation, and indicated that no allocation would be available for additional new units in 1983.
Cityhome wanted to develop 964 units in 1983. The Commissioner of Housing believed the Province would support the building of over 600 units. These units would be located at 27 Elm Street, Elizabeth and Chestnut, Bathurst Quay, Greenwood and Walpole, Coxwell Stables, Jones and Curzon, Jarvis and Homewood and Queen and Vanauley. Construction of those 964 units would result in over 2,000 person years of employment.
We in this Party believe the Province of Ontario should be expanding the municipal non-profit housing sector, not cutting it back. We will continue to argue for a major infusion of new funds into the co-operative and non-profit sector to create jobs and meet our housing needs. When we take a look at the actual cost savings, apart from the social benefits to society, we find that to keep an individual in an institution costs upwards of $30,000 per year. To allow that person to live within the mainstream of Canadian life in the community, the cost to the taxpayer is something around $8,000 per year. This is a substantial saving to the taxpayer and provides the disabled person or the psychiatric patient upon his discharge from an institution with an opportunity to become a fully participating member of society again.
It is not so long ago that we in Canada observed the International Year of Disabled Persons. In fact, the House recognized the importance of that international year by establishing a Task Force comprised of Members of all political parties in the House to conduct an investigation into the needs of the disabled in this country.
One of the major findings of that Task Force was the crying need for deinstitutionalized programs for disabled people in the country. I am not talking about the kind of deinstitutionalization that has taken place in Ontario, where literally thousands of mental patients are being discharged from care centres into the community without adequate community support bases being provided. There is a particular need for adequate housing for those phychiatric patients who have been discharged. I am now talking about the kind of deinstitutionalized program that is taking place in the Province of Ontario where there is an intention to close homes for the mentally retarded. I am sure that the inadequate housing that will be provided for these patients will be of less benefit to them than the existing accommodation.
If the Government were to ask the House for authority to borrow funds for these socially useful purposes, I am sure that Members on this side would not be as reluctant as we are to give the Government the authority to borrow that sizeable amount of money. We hear talk about deinstitutionalization and the cost of keeping people in institutions as opposed to allowing them to live in the community.

Borrowing Authority
If the Government were to say that it wanted to use these moneys for job-creation projects, housing construction and socially-useful purposes, I may feel an awful lot easier about giving that authority. Today I do not.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that happens to be an embarrassing question because I cannot answer without reservation, except to say that I was under the impression that at no time had I spoken on any aspect of the borrowing Bill, that is to say, Bill C-143. I am virtually certain that I did not, but at the same time I can just as easily assure the Chair that the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) probably spoke on the Bill. With that situation and in the absence of any objection from Hon. Members, I will proceed.
In ten minutes it is very difficult to express with any satisfactory result one's view of the provision in Bill C-143 which authorizes a further borrowing that in total amounts to $19 billion. It is one of the simplest provisions before the House of Commons, but at the same time it is one that has the greatest possible ramifications for the people of Canada. To try to put into real terms the effect of a massive legislative measure such as an authority to borrow $19 billion, let me point out that this borrowing and other anticipated borrowings will bring the total debt load of the Government of Canada into the area of $200 billion. If we divide that among the people of Canada, we will see immediately that every man, woman and child will owe, as a result of all this borrowing, some $8,000; that is $8,000 for every Canadian person.
When we attribute that borrowing to the work force in Canada-the people who actually have to pay the bills and provide the wealth and resources to the Government which enables it to carry on its services and pay for its debt-we realize that the debt more than doubles. Every working Canadian can look forward to carrying on behalf of the Government of Canada a debt load of some $18,000 and to paying and providing the resources to pay the interest on that amount of debt.
When we look back a year or so ago when the interest rate was at 19 per cent, we realize the enormity of that burden on the people of Canada. Unfortunately it does not end there because each of us lives in one of the Provinces of Canada, in the Northwest Territories or in Yukon. In respect of that residence we have, as wage earners and supporters of the economy of the country, a liability to support our Provinces. That carries with it an additional burden. For example, in the case of the Province of Nova Scotia, my obligation as a
resident apparently is to pay $5,224 in addition to the $18,000 that I owe as a wage earner of Canada. If we increase that number proportionately, we find that my debt load is not only the $18,000 with which I have to support Canada, but the $10,000 or more which I have to supply in respect of my obligations to the Province of Nova Scotia.
I could almost sit down now because the thought of owing $26,000 on top of every other responsibility of a wage earner in Canada is of such magnitude and so horrendous that it dispels and dissipates every ambition for economic success in the future. This is exactly what has happened in Canada. We have become victims of our own extravagance. But it is not our extravagance as individual Canadians; it is the extravagance of the Government of Canada. It did not learn the lesson which was learned by Canadians in the post-war period after 1945 and in the early 1950s. I remember as a university student in that period reading a reproduction of an editorial which appeared in the New York Times, in which the Government of Canada was praised for not only balancing the budget, that is to say equating the expenditures of the Government of Canada to its income and revenues, but providing a tidy surplus. It was not a great amount, but it was enough to put aside for the proverbial rainy day. Since the heydays of the early 1950s, the attitude of the Government of Canada changed very drastically and it got completely away from the idea and concept of a balanced budget.
I just want to take a minute or two to address myself to the concept of a balanced budget. Many people say that that is a right-wing view, that it is the view of arch-capitalists that we have to balance our expenditures against our income. It is a rule of economics that we cannot deny regardless of our other views. It is a fact of economic life that if one allows one's expenditures to exceed one's income and revenues, one will get in difficulty somewhere along the line. It is not only those who want to be economic purists who respect the concept of a balanced budget. It is also those who want to provide a future for all Canadians and to provide the services which all Canadians need right now. The only method to ensure the provision of social services is to have the kind of economic purity which results from a balanced budget.
We in the House of Commons have to remind the Government of Canada constantly that having abandoned this essential and necessary economic concept, it now has to recognize and realize the error of its ways and return to that concept. Until we bring back into the economic and governmental affairs of Canada the concept of a balanced budget, we will remain in the economic no man's land in which we have been drifting for the past decade and in which, of necessity, we will have to drift for another decade.
Just as I favour the concept of a balanced budget, I recognize that we cannot return to that concept overnight because we have made a social contract and have guaranteed to the people of Canada that we will provide necessary medical services, hospital care, and education, in some circumstances at no cost and in other circumstances at a tuition fee. We have to continue these kinds of services, but at the same time our challenge and task is to bring all this into line, that is to say,
March 14, 1983

the concept of a balanced budget and the necessity for continuing social services, including health care, education and all the services to which Canadians have become accustomed.
The other side of the coin is that in falling into the horror of continual deficit budgeting we have built up an economic burden that we can no longer carry. I have heard from time to time that the Government of Canada has said to provincial leaders that they must take up more of the economic burden. As I have already indicated, it would appear to me that practically every Province of Canada has reached the limit of its financial capacity as well. For instance, every resident of New Brunswick carries a debt of $6,200. In Newfoundland, the per capita debt is $6,300. Even in rich Ontario the per capita debt is $4,060, and in Quebec it is $4,500. I could go on with these statistics, but they merely point out the facts that Canadians, who are not only residents of Canada but residents of the Provinces and Territories of Canada, have reached the limit of their debt capacity and that this spending spree has to stop.
When the former Minister of Finance introduced his budget he gave the indication that the spending spree was going to stop, that he was bringing forward a program of restraint in Government spending which he called the six and five program. He immediately took the dollar bills that were saved as a result of the six and five program and assigned them to other areas of Government expenditure. The net result was even greater Government spending and an increase in the deficit.
The deficit has risen over the past two years from $11 billion to $19 billion, to $23.6 billion to $26 billion, and now it is nearing $29 billion. As long as we attempt to carry a deficit of that size, every social service and every educational service is in danger. But the spending goes on and on.
Last week we learned that the Canadian National Railway has piled up a deficit of $225 million. That was after spinning off all the loss operations, such as CN Marine and VIA Rail. When will it all stop? When will the Michael Pitfields stop feeding at the public trough? When will all this spending stop? What we are doing here is dealing with this Bill and with this amendment and trying to convince the Government that it has to stop its spending, that it deals with the realities of Government expenditure and service, and get Canada back on the road to a balanced budget.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to hear that my colleague from Nipissing, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) will be listening attentively.
Once again, I want to rise to speak to this appalling Bill. Bill C-143 is in itself such an outright admission of fiscal and administrative failure that in our parliamentary system as practised anywhere but in Ottawa under the Liberal Party of Canada it would only be presented if accompanied by the resignation of the Government responsible.
We all know now that because Liberals feel no guilt they, therefore, have no guilt. Out of the goodness of my heart, let me present them with a slogan that might or might not serve them well in the next election. It is: "Being a Liberal means never having to say you're guilty."
Therefore, before the beginning of the new fiscal year, before we have so much as seen a budget-and I would remind you that when this Bill was introduced we had not even seen the Estimates-and before we are given any idea what the money is wanted for, we are being forced to authorize a blank cheque for $19 billion.
Let me use what I think is a very graphic illustration to give some idea of just what we are talking about when we glibly toss around phrases like "$19 billion." If your ancestors and mine had started a company in the year Jesus was born, capitalizing it with $1 billion but, running it so badly that it lost $1,000 a day, we would today still have a quarter of our capital left. That is $ 1 billion.
O)
This Bill tells us that the Government wants us to give it a blank cheque for $19 billion, $5 billion of which is to paper over its various sins of omissions of this fiscal year and another $14 billion to get it well under way to its undisclosed and uncertain destination in fiscal year 1983-84.
Let us look at what little we do know about Government spending plans for the coming year. Let us see if they are the stuff that gives us any spine stiffening confidence that our moneys are being well husbanded and sparingly spent. Bear in mind that this is the Government which has just forced its six and five regime on its pensioners and the senior citizens of the nation. Yet, it has allowed the salary and wage costs in the Ministry of Economic Development, for example, to rise by
52.3 per cent. This cannot be due merely to new recruiting because the manpower of the Department has gone up by only 3 per cent. It is hard to see how it can be due to a reorganization of functions in the economic area because at the same time the salaries of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion have risen by 9.1 per cent and those of Industry, Trade and Commerce, by 8.4 per cent. Indeed, wages and salaries in the Government as a whole have gone up by 7.6 per cent which, by comparison with the Government's past standards, is pretty good. However, in comparison with what could and should be achieved by an administration for which fiscal responsibility is something more than a slogan and in comparison with the Government's own six and five guidelines, it is an affront.
If a Government comes to this House and asks for a blank cheque for $19 billion, at least we should be assured that its estimating and forecasting is accurate. Let us look at what its estimates tell us about the coming year's construction costs. We must presume that some of this money will go to pay construction costs, but we do not know that.
The Ministry of Transport is building a firehall and garage at St. John's National Airport and is making some modifications on the air terminal at the Regina National Airport. The previous Estimates for these came to $40.4 million. This year's Estimates come to $78.2 million, which is an increase of 93.6 per cent.
What about our new embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia? Last year its cost was estimated at $1.7 million. The latest guess is $32.8 million, which is an increase of 1,829 per cent. So it goes. The costs of Canadian police services facilities at Rockliffe, St. John's and Fredericton are up by 59.6 per cent.
Let us turn to the classic place for hiding sins of omission, standard item No. 12 which is "other expenditures". This item is up by 88.4 per cent this year. What does that mean? I guess we will have to wait for the debate on the Estimates and hope for an explanation then. In the meanwhile, we are expected to pass a blank cheque Bill for $19 billion, part of which moneys will presumably be spent on this item, whatever it may represent. In any event, we are told that none of that is any of our business and that we should just shut up and pass the legislation. It goes without saying that this kind of legislative conduct is bad for the political system. It goes without saying that this sort of catch-up financial fumble ball is the mark of an exhausted Government which is out of control of the public purse, out of touch with the public mood, and out of sync with economic realities. Yet, as long as its tame sheep will bleat on demand, the Government remains in control of the House and this Bill will pass.
When I look across the aisle, I think of the line in "HMS Pinafore", sung by Sir Joseph Porter, KCB, which is:
I always voted at my party's call and never thought of thinking for myself at all-
And the next line, which you will remember:
I thought so little they rewarded me-
And so on. How little times seem to have changed, in Liberal Ottawa anyway.
March 14, 1983

There is a line spoken by Sir Winston Churchill in "Churchill; the Wilderness Years" which was shown in recent weeks on the PBS System. Mr. Churchill had at least been offered a Cabinet post by Neville Chamberlain after being resolutely ignored for a decade because of his independent views. Mr. Chamberlain expressed regret for this, and Sir Winston replied that as long as Party discipline is not so tight as to stifle honest dissent, democracy is safe. I am wondering if we will see that here in Ottawa.
Of course, this Bill will pass because it must. It will be passed because the Government, which has lost control of the country and the public purse, retains control of the legislature. As a result, democracy is ill served.
It is clear that while it may technically retain the confidence of this House, it has forfeited the confidence of mainstreet Canada, and this Bill and what it represents is why.
It is wrong in principle to force through a draft for any sum to pay for God knows what and move the country further along God knows what undisclosed path. It is wrong by every standard of measurement to purloin $19 billion from the taxpaying public.
I want to say to those who heretofore have been very acquiescent on the other side of the House and who are willing to give the Bill the stamp of endorsement that the great public, their electorate and mine, whose money they are taking, are watching them now. They must now pass judgment on this, their Government's Bill. Of course, I know that the people of Canada will make their decision later.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to take part in this debate and speak against a Bill which would allow the Government to borrow $19 billion. Many speakers have tried to explain what $19 billion is. I believe, when speaking to the amendment approximately a week ago, I indicated that, at least by my arithmetic, it would take a husband and wife 53,000 years to spend $19 billion at the rate of $1,000 a day, seven days a week.
I would like to make a couple of points in the ten minutes that I have. They deal primarily with the question of waste in proportions which I think would make any democracy in the history of the world blush. Let me give a few examples, for which I am indebted to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke) since these examples come from one of his recent householders. My first example, remember, comes from the Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). It is a plane ticket for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), which cost the ordinary taxpayer $2,611, so that he could fly by Concord Jet on June 14, 1982, from Kennedy Airport to Heath row in London. I did not have time to check what the regular airfare is but I am prepared to wager that it would be much less than the $2,611 that is required of those who have the taste to fly by Concord.
My second example involves photocopying. The Auditor General tells us that the federal Government spends in excess of $50 million each year currently for photocopying, for approximately $900 million photocopies per year.
Borrowing Authority
The third example of absolute, total waste is the $674,000 spent to buy briefcases for public servants between April of 1980 and June of 1981.
The fourth example relates to land banking. The Government spent $775 million in land banking for future Canadian housing needs. According to the 1978 Greenspan Report on land prices, instead of controlling land prices, the program created a shortage of land, providing spectacular profits for land speculators as prices skyrocketed.
The next example is the promotion of the six and five. That is the restraint program, as Hon. Members will remember. How there is a connection between six and five and the Canada Unity Information office is beyond me. The Government spent $1 million to set up exhibits at the Canadian National Exhibition, the Pacific National Exhibition and Expo Quebec. I might add, since I am dealing with the Unity Information office, that I am advised that the Government spent $4,500 last month to advertise "the Crow goes without a flap" in the Montreal Gazette. That was the ad which told us that westerners would not benefit from the abolition of the Crow rate.
The sixth example of unparalleled waste is the fact that the Auditor General told us not long ago that the net debt of the Government of Canada is understated by $14.5 billion as of March 31, 1982. Oh, the list becomes very long.
The 1981 Canada Savings Bond issue had a $1 billion blunder in it. As Hon. Members will recall, these geniuses of finance opposite decided to offer the bond issue at 19.5 per cent interest, and the economist, Donald McGillivray, has estimated that, based on the interest rates prevailing at the time, the cost to the taxpayer was a mere extra $1 billion more than was necessary.
I cannot resist the example of the Jet Stars flying in formation to Winnipeg. That was when Messrs. Munro, Gray and Blais used three separate Jet Stars to fly to the same Liberal fund raising dinner in Winnipeg. Indeed, the cost of fuel alone would have been $27,000, and first class commercial airline tickets would have cost $1,770, return.

Mr. Speaker, I know, as I was saying it, that I was making a mistake. I hope that Your Honour will forgive me. I notice that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) did not tell us whether or not he went to the fund raising dinner.
The next item which I would mention concerns the question of the $200,000, I believe, which is being paid in salaries, benefits, travel allowances or expenses, to keep Mr. Edwin Clark in Paris for a year with his family in the style to which he has become accustomed. I do not believe that there are very many people opposite who will stand and defend that particular use of the taxpayer's money.
I suppose that my favourite example, because everyone in Canada can relate to it, concerns the $ 11,000 which the Government spent to send Miss Janet Smith from the Privy Council office to study French on the Riviera in France. Do you know how the Government defended it, Mr. Speaker? It stated that paying to send this young lady to take French lessons in Quebec, New Brunswick, Ottawa or anywhere else would require a cash outlay of $13,000, I believe. In other words, Canadian taxpayers were being saved, by some perverted bit of logic, the sum of $2,000. If one ignores our balance of payments problems, it just might make sense, but not otherwise.

I should like to switch to French now to mention a few points raised by University of Montreal Professor Maurice Marchon about current problems related to inflation and unemployment. Here is what he said about our situation over the past ten years:
The Canadian experience at the beginning of this decade has some similarities with the Swiss and Japanese experiences. The Bank of Canada intervention on the money market in 1971-72 and the fact that interest rates were kept too low resulted in a money supply expansion rate which was not conducive to price stability. The national product growth rate was very high in 1971-72, but inflation reached 11 per cent in 1974. The rapid increase in the inflation rate cannot therefore be due mainly to rising energy prices controlled by the Government, but above all to an overly expansionary monetary policy.

He continues and basically says, as I understand his writing, that the Government does not understand monetarism or the proper use of the theories of John Maynard Keynes.
Concerning the problem we have now, I refer to some points made by Professor Antonio Martino, Professor of Monetary History at the University of Rome, in an excellent book entitled "Constraining Inflationary Government". One of his points, which is totally germane to what we are discussing now, is that Government deficits reach a very high level and they
inevitably lead to "refinancing of the deficit through money creation". That is happening now and will continue to happen.
Professor Martino quotes Richard Wagner and Robert Tollis on the same point as saying, "While some Government borrowing is for investment, most of it is for consumption. This means that budget deficits replace the creation of capital goods with a subsidization of consumption". Further down, he quotes Walter Eltis as saying, "It must be particularly disturbing to Keynesian policy-makers that the countries where the influence has been greatest are those which have suffered most from inflation". Further down, in his concluding paragraph, he discusses inflation. In effect, he says that Keynes' obsession with the short-run was also doomed to result in both destabilizing macroeconomic policies and in an inflationary bias. He discussed how Keynes' policies have destroyed the most effective constraint in Government growth. At one point it was considered undesirable to have a deficit. Now it has become a desirable feature.
I must tell Hon. Members that our deficit this year is on the order of $26 billion. It is rather like a pyramid. It becomes larger every year. The point that Hon. Members opposite cannot comprehend is that the more they create deficits, the more they create additional problems for taxpayers in servicing the debt, and we will have even more unemployment. As evident in today's Gallup poll, unemployment is now, by far the largest problem for Canadians.
It is like talking to the trees. They do not listen. Like the Bourbon kings, they neither listen, learn nor forget. I suppose it is obvious that I wish they would bring on an election so that we could change to a Government which believed in people instead of larger and larger deficits.

Mr. Speaker, in this debate we have heard a number of definitions of the quantity of money which is being requested in this legislation, the $5 billion for current expenditures and the $14 billion for future expenditures, unspecified, and for purposes which are not clear. Regarding the $19 billion that are contained in this Bill, it is worth recalling that in the Estimates that were tabled about 10 days ago a table, Chart B at page 9, indicated the various envelopes under which the expenditures for the year are foreseen. With respect to the public debt, we are talking about indebtedness and future indebtedness, and I am thinking of the pages that are sitting in front of you, Mr. Speaker, and the debt that is going to be on their heads. We are borrowing; they are going to pay. Let us remember that. That applies to the children of every person in this room, in this Chamber, and across this country. Their children are going to be faced with repaying the debt that we are being asked to authorize here.
That $19 billion, to come back to the table, Chart B on page 9 of the Estimates, indicates that the debt servicing this year is going to amount to $18.57 billion. In other words, what the Government is trying to borrow now would just about meet the servicing of the current debt. We are being asked to increase that debt so that next year that amount of money would not
March 14, 1983

service the debt, that is, the settlement of outstanding loans, the rescheduling and also paying the interest.
Furthermore, it is worth remembering that over the past six years the percentage of the degree of servicing the public debt has actually doubled. In 1977-78, the amount required for servicing the public debt was $5.5 billion. Today it is $18.57 billion. It has more than trebled. On the average over those six years, that is a 12 per cent inflation factor. Our indebtedness has been increasing at the rate of 12 per cent per year. We hear the Government boasting, puffing out their chests and saying, "What great boys we are because we have brought down the inflation rate." They are increasing the inflation rate because the average increase in indebtedness over these six years is 12 per cent.
A number of Members have been trying to provide a means of comprehending the size of the borrowing authority that we are dealing with today, the $19 billion. I have tried to reduce it to actual physical scale, and I do not know whether you, Mr. Speaker, have ever seen a stack of $1,000 bills all gathered up together with a piece of paper around them. A thousand of those $1,000 bills would make a million dollars, and that would be only four inches thick. Three million dollars, if they were stacked on top of one another would make a stack one foot high, and that is only three million dollars. The Peace Tower is about 300 feet high and if they were stacked up in front of the Peace Tower, by the time the look-out point was reached with stacks of $1,000 bills a total of $1 billion would not have been reached. And we are talking about $19 billion. If we wanted to have all of those $1,000 bills stacked in front of the House of Commons it would make quite a sight, would it not? Nineteen columns of $1 billion each sitting side by side. The main entrance to the House of Commons would be blocked by the $1,000 bills that we are being asked to authorize in this Bill. It is preposterous.
If we put it another way, if we stacked them all the way up, they would reach to over 6,000 feet, 6,333 feet is the exact figure, and that is, as close as I can make it, about two kilometres, for those who prefer to speak in kilometres. We have a column two kilometres high of $1,000 bills, and that is the scale of this particular operation.
Put in another way, where could one find such funds? Let us say they were spread equally amongst all of the constituencies of this country. There are 282 constituencies. That would mean that each constituency would be responsible for raising $67.3 million. To make it even more impressive, $67.3 million in some constituencies perhaps would be no great problem, but let us look at it in terms of Prince Edward Island. Those four constituencies in Prince Edward Island-and I am sorry that the Minister is not here to realize what his Government is asking this Parliament to do-would be required to raise $269.5 million. I do not think the banks on Prince Edward Island could raise that unless they were given some notice, and therefore that gives us a notion of the magnitude in terms of constituencies.
In terms of population, what does it mean? Here again I refer to the pages. They, and everyone in this country, are under an obligation, if that amount of money is to be raised,
Borrowing Authority
$19 billion, to find $750 and put it out on the table there and say: "Okay, Government, there is your $19 billion." That is preposterous. In terms of families, it means about $750 for every man, woman and child, and if you deal with that on the basis of, let us say, a family of four, that means $3,000 for a family of four. Every family of four in this country would be required to find $3,000 to make up this sum.
Because of the nature of Clauses 2 and 3, one being the requirement for $5 billion for current expenditures and the other one for $14 billion, I do hope that when this goes to committee we will be able to introduce an amendment which will split the Bill so that we will leave the $14 billion to one side until the year in which it is to be spent appears and until we have some notion from the Government as to the manner in which it proposes to spend those funds.
That is my case. It is a lot of money. It could block the doorway to the Peace Tower. It would require Prince Edward Island to raise almost $270 million. It puts at the door of every Canadian the requirement to raise $750. That is a preposterous notion when you consider that $14 billion of that is for purposes of which we have no notion whatsoever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those persons who have lost their jobs, their homes or their businesses and those who are now unemployed and those trying to enter the labour market for the first time have awakened to the size and magnitude of Government financial operations. In other words they are more conscious of taxes and spending than ever before. What concerns most people I talk to about Bill C-143 is the process by which it is being handled. We have this situation. The Government wants to borrow $19 billion, $5 billion for use between now and March 31 and $14 billion for future requirements.
What we want to see is a projection of revenue and expenditures before we approve the borrowing of the $14 billion. It does not seem to be an unusual request. Anyone with any sense of responsibility for financial matters would want to know revenue and expenditure levels before loans of the magnitude of $19 billion were undertaken.
There is no doubt that the people of Canada just do not trust the Government and the process it uses. The raising of taxes, the approval of spending Estimates and the lack of forecasting for future expenditures is very much in question in the minds of the people of Canada today. The people of this country want some assurance that the pipeline has a valve that will meter the flow.
The feeling is that if we do not watch the process closely, those who sacrifice to bring down inflation will have done so for nothing. In other words, we are on a narrow path. If we walk carefully, we can make it safely out of the inflation and recession that we are enduring. If not, we are in difficulty. Part of the walking carefully is knowing where we are going.
We and people generally would be happy and would view it as being more acceptable if we saw a new budget and then the borrowing authority brought in later. In other words, let us see

March 14, 1983
Borrowing Authority
what our revenue will be to cover the $89 billion proposed in the spending Estimates. Let us see the estimated shortfall, and then we will look at the borrowing requirements.
Three Auditors General in a row have said that Government spending is out of control. Numerous boards and commissions have said the same. Just contemplate the magnitude of the Estimates, $88.9 billion, a 17 per cent increase over the Main Estimates of last year. That is not the end of it. We will have Supplementary Estimates A, B, C, D, E and F. We do not know what it will come to. We do not know how much more spending will be done and how high the amount will go before we are asked to approve another borrowing authority beyond the $19 billion.
If we look at the budgetary deficits, we see a picture of deficits which began at $5 billion in 1975-76. It went to $6.2 billion, then to $10.3 billion, onwards and onwards until we have approximately $30 billion by March 31 of this year. With that record, no wonder there is a lack of trust between the people of Canada and their Government. Since 1980, the Government has run up $90 billion in deficits. Those who are trying to rearrange their lives from the effects of the recession-and there is no one who has not been hurt by the recession-those who have been ravaged by high interest rates and are carrying a heavy debt load live in fear that inflation will return and they will have another round of the same.
We have an opportunity to put back into our national affairs a measure of confidence, no matter how small it may be. We should have a forecast of revenues and expenditures together with an anticipated borrowing for five years ahead. Other Governments do it. Large corporations forecast long and short-range. There is no reason in the world why it cannot be done here. We should begin here now.
